knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
It suffices to show the following general result:

There exists a constant \( c > 0 \) depending only on the dimension, and constants \( {C}_{q} \) depending only on the dimension and \( q \) and bounds \( {B}_{j} \) on the curvature and its derivatives for \( j \leq  q \) where \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {B}_{j} \) , so that for any metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) , we have

\[
\frac{1}{2}{I}_{k\ell } \leq  {g}_{k\ell } \leq  2{I}_{k\ell }
\]

and

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{1}}}\cdots \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{q}}}{g}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}
\]

where \( {I}_{k\ell } \) is the Euclidean metric.

Suppose we are given a metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( x\right) d{x}^{i}d{x}^{j} \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) as in Claim 1. Then by definition every line through the origin is a geodesic (parametrized proportional to arc length) and \( {g}_{ij} = {I}_{ij} \) at the origin. Also, the Gauss Lemma says that the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is in geodesic coordinates if and only if \( {g}_{ij}{x}^{i} = {I}_{ij}{x}^{i} \) . Note in particular that in geodesic coordinates

\[
{\left| x\right| }^{2} = {g}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j} = {I}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j}
\]

is unambiguously defined. Also, in geodesic coordinates we have \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) , and all the first derivatives for \( {g}_{jk} \) vanish at the origin.

Introduce the symmetric tensor

\[
{A}_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}{x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}{g}_{ij}.
\]

Since we have \( {g}_{jk}{x}^{k} = {I}_{jk}{x}^{k} \) , we get

\[
{x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{g}_{jk} = {I}_{ij} - {g}_{ij} = {x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}{g}_{ik}
\]

and hence from the formula for \( {\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} \)

\[
{x}^{j}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} = {g}^{i\ell }{A}_{k\ell }
\]

Hence \( {A}_{k\ell }{x}^{k} = 0 \) . Let \( {D}_{i} \) be the covariant derivative with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) . Then

\[
{D}_{i}{x}^{k} = {I}_{i}^{k} + {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{x}^{j} = {I}_{i}^{k} + {g}^{k\ell }{A}_{i\ell }.
\]

Introduce the potential function

\[
P = {\left| x\right| }^{2}/2 = \frac{1}{2}{g}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j}.
\]

We can use the formulas above to compute

\[
{D}_{i}P = {g}_{ij}{x}^{j}.
\]

Also we get

\[
{D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij}.
\]

The defining equation for \( P \) gives

\[
{g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}P = {2P}.
\]

If we take the covariant derivative of this equation we get

\[
{g}^{k\ell }{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{\ell }P = {D}_{j}P
\]

which is equivalent to \( {A}_{jk}{x}^{k} = 0 \) . But if we take the covariant derivative again we get

\[
{g}^{k\ell }{D}_{i}{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{\ell }P + {g}^{k\ell }{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{i}{D}_{\ell }P = {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P.
\]

Now switching derivatives

\[
{D}_{i}{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P = {D}_{i}{D}_{k}{D}_{j}P = {D}_{k}{D}_{i}{D}_{j}P + {R}_{{ikj}\ell }{g}^{\ell m}{D}_{m}P
\]

and if we use this and \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) and \( {g}^{k\ell }{D}_{\ell }P = {x}^{k} \) we find that

\[
{x}^{k}{D}_{k}{A}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} + {g}^{k\ell }{A}_{ik}{A}_{j\ell } + {R}_{{ikj}\ell }{x}^{k}{x}^{\ell } = 0.
\]

From our assumed curvature bounds we can take \( \left| {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\right|  \leq  {B}_{0} \) . Then we get the following estimate:

\[
\left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}{A}_{ij} + {A}_{ij}}\right|  \leq  C{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

on the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) for some constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension.

We now show how to use the maximum principle on such equations. First of all, by a maximum principle argument, it is easy to show that if \( f \) is a function on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) and \( \lambda  > 0 \) is a constant, then

\[
\lambda \sup \left| f\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}^{k}} + {\lambda f}}\right| .
\]

For any tensor \( T = \left\{  {T}_{i\cdots j}\right\} \) and any constant \( \lambda  > 0 \) , setting \( f = {\left| T\right| }^{2} \) in the above inequality, we have

(4.1.8)

\[
\lambda \sup \left| T\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}T + {\lambda T}}\right| .
\]

Applying this to the tensor \( {A}_{ij} \) we get

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  C\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

for some constant depending only on the dimension.

It is fairly elementary to see that there exist constants \( c > 0 \) and \( {C}_{0} < \infty \) such that if the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is in geodesic coordinates with \( \left| {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\right|  \leq  {B}_{0} \) in the ball of radius \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) then

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2}.
\]

Indeed, since the derivatives of \( {g}_{ij} \) vanish at the origin, so does \( {A}_{ij} \) . Hence the estimate holds near the origin. But the inequality

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  C\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

says that \( \left| {A}_{ij}\right| \) avoids an interval when \( c \) is chosen small. In fact the inequality

\[
X \leq  C{X}^{2} + D
\]

is equivalent to

\[
\left| {{2CX} - 1}\right|  \geq  \sqrt{1 - {4CD}}
\]

which makes \( X \) avoid an interval if \( {4CD} < 1 \) . (Hence in our case we need to choose \( c \) with \( 4{C}^{2}{c}^{2} < 1 \) .) Then if \( X \) is on the side containing 0 we get

\[
X \leq  \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - {4CD}}}{2C} \leq  {2D}.
\]

This gives \( \left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2} \) with \( {C}_{0} = {2C} \) .

We can also derive bounds on all the covariant derivatives of \( P \) in terms of bounds on the covariant derivatives of the curvature. To simplify the notation, we let

\[
{D}^{q}P = \left\{  {{D}_{{j}_{1}}{D}_{{j}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}P}\right\}
\]

denote the \( {q}^{\text{ th }} \) covariant derivative, and in estimating \( {D}^{q}P \) we will lump all the lower order terms into a general slush term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) which will be a polynomial in \( {D}^{1}P,{D}^{2}P,\ldots ,{D}^{q - 1}P \) and \( {Rm},{D}^{1}{Rm},\ldots ,{D}^{q - 2}{Rm} \) . We already have estimates on a ball of radius \( r \)

\[
P \leq  {r}^{2}/2
\]

\[
\left| {{D}^{1}P}\right|  \leq  r
\]

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

and since \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) and \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) if we choose \( c \) small we can make

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  1/2
\]

and we get

\[
\left| {{D}^{2}P}\right|  \leq  {C}_{2}
\]

for some constant \( {C}_{2} \) depending only on the dimension.

Start with the equation \( {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}P = {2P} \) and apply repeated covariant derivatives. Observe that we get an equation which starts out

\[
{g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}^{q}{D}_{j}P + \cdots  = 0
\]

where the omitted terms only contain derivatives \( {D}^{q}P \) and lower. If we switch two derivatives in a term \( {D}^{q + 1}P \) or lower, we get a term which is a product of a covariant derivative of \( {Rm} \) of order at most \( q - 2 \) (since the two closest to \( P \) commute) and a covariant derivative of \( P \) of order at most \( q - 1 \) ; such a term can be lumped in with the slush term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) . Therefore up to terms in \( {\Phi }^{q} \) we can regard the derivatives as commuting. Then paying attention to the derivatives in \( {D}^{1}P \) we get an equation

\( {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{1}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P \; + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{2}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}{D}_{{k}_{3}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + \cdots  + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{q}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q - 1}}P \; = {D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + {\Phi }^{q}. \)

Recalling that \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) we can rewrite this as

\[
{\Phi }^{q} = {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}} + \left( {q - 1}\right) {D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P
\]

\[
+ {g}^{ij}{A}_{i{k}_{1}}{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + \cdots  + {g}^{ij}{A}_{i{k}_{q}}{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q - 1}}P.
\]

Estimating the product of tensors in the usual way gives

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{D}^{q}P + \left( {q - 1}\right) {D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  q\left| A\right| \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  + \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right| .
\]

Applying the inequality \( \lambda \sup \left| T\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}T + {\lambda T}}\right| \) with \( T = {D}^{q}P \) gives

\[
\left( {q - 1}\right) \sup \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  \sup \left( {q\left| A\right| \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  + \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right| }\right) .
\]

Now we can make \( \left| A\right|  \leq  1/2 \) by making \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) with \( c \) small; it is important here that \( c \) is independent of \( q \) ! Then we get

\[
\left( {q - 2}\right) \sup \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  2\sup \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right|
\]

which is a good estimate for \( q \geq  3 \) . The term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) is estimated inductively from the terms \( {D}^{q - 1}P \) and \( {D}^{q - 2}{Rm} \) and lower. This proves that there exist constants \( {C}_{q} \) for \( q \geq  3 \) depending only on \( q \) and the dimension and on \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right| \) for \( j \leq  q - 2 \) such that

\[
\left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}
\]

on the ball \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) .

Now we turn our attention to estimating the Euclidean metric \( {I}_{jk} \) and its covariant derivatives with respect to \( {g}_{jk} \) . We will need the following elementary fact: suppose that \( f \) is a function on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) with \( f\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}^{i}}}\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Then

(4.1.9)

\[
\left| f\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for the same constant \( C \) . As a consequence, if \( T = \left\{  {T}_{j\cdots k}\right\} \) is a tensor which vanishes at the origin and if

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}T}\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) then \( \left| T\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2} \) with the same constant \( C \) . (Simply apply the inequality (4.1.9) to the function \( f = \left| T\right| \) . In case this is not smooth, we can use \( f = \sqrt{{\left| T\right| }^{2} + {\epsilon }^{2}} - \epsilon \) and then let \( \epsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) .)

Our application will be to the tensor \( {I}_{jk} \) which gives the Euclidean metric as a tensor in geodesic coordinates. We have

\[
{D}_{i}{I}_{jk} =  - {\Gamma }_{ij}^{p}{I}_{pk} - {\Gamma }_{ik}^{p}{I}_{pj}
\]

and since

\[
{x}^{i}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{p} = {g}^{pq}{A}_{jq}
\]

we get the equation

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{I}_{jk} =  - {g}^{pq}{A}_{jp}{I}_{kq} - {g}^{pq}{A}_{kp}{I}_{jq}.
\]

We already have \( \left| {A}_{jk}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2} \) for \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) . The tensor \( {I}_{jk} \) doesn’t vanish at the origin, but the tensor

\[
{h}_{jk} = {I}_{jk} - {g}_{jk}
\]

does. We can then use

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{h}_{jk} =  - {g}^{pq}{A}_{jp}{h}_{kq} - {g}^{pq}{A}_{kq}{h}_{jq} - 2{A}_{jk}.
\]

Suppose \( M\left( s\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  s}}\left| {h}_{jk}\right| \) . Then

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{h}_{jk}}\right|  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

and we get

\[
\left| {h}_{jk}\right|  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

on \( \left| x\right|  \leq  s \) . This makes

\[
M\left( s\right)  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2}.
\]

Then for \( s \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) with \( c \) small compared to \( {C}_{0} \) we get \( 2{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2} \leq  1/2 \) and \( M\left( s\right)  \leq  4{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2} \) . Thus

\[
\left| {{I}_{jk} - {g}_{jk}}\right|  = \left| {h}_{jk}\right|  \leq  4{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) , and hence for \( c \) small enough

\[
\frac{1}{2}{g}_{jk} \leq  {I}_{jk} \leq  2{g}_{jk}
\]

Thus the metrics are comparable. Note that this estimate only needs \( r \) small compared to \( {B}_{0} \) and does not need any bounds on the derivatives of the curvature.

Now to obtain bounds on the covariant derivative of the Eucliden metric \( {I}_{k\ell } \) with respect to the Riemannian metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) we want to start with the equation

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{I}_{k\ell } + {g}^{mn}{A}_{km}{I}_{\ell n} + {g}^{mn}{A}_{\ell m}{I}_{kn} = 0
\]

and apply \( q \) covariant derivatives \( {D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}} \) . Each time we do this we must interchange \( {D}_{j} \) and \( {x}^{i}{D}_{i} \) , and since this produces a term which helps we should look at it closely. If we write \( {R}_{ji} = \left\lbrack  {{D}_{j},{D}_{i}}\right\rbrack \) for the commutator, this operator on tensors involves the curvature but no derivatives. Since

\[
{D}_{j}{x}^{i} = {I}_{j}^{i} + {g}^{im}{A}_{jm}
\]

we can compute

\[
\left\lbrack  {{D}_{j},{x}^{i}{D}_{i}}\right\rbrack   = {D}_{j} + {g}^{im}{A}_{jm}{D}_{i} + {x}^{i}{R}_{ji}
\]

and the term \( {D}_{j} \) in the commutator helps, while \( {A}_{jm} \) can be kept small and \( {R}_{ji} \) is zero order. It follows that we get an equation of the form

\[
0 = {x}^{i}{D}_{i}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell } + q{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{h = 1}}^{q}{g}^{im}{A}_{{j}_{h}m}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{h - 1}}{D}_{i}{D}_{{j}_{h + 1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }
\]

\[
+ {g}^{mn}{A}_{km}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{\ell n} + {g}^{mn}{A}_{\ell m}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{kn} + {\Psi }^{q},
\]

where the slush term \( {\Psi }^{q} \) is a polynomial in derivatives of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) of degree no more than \( q - 1 \) and derivatives of \( P \) of degree no more than \( q + 2 \) (remember \( {x}^{i} = {g}^{ij}{D}_{j}P \) and \( {A}_{ij} = {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P - {g}_{ij} \) ) and derivatives of the curvature \( {Rm} \) of degree no more than \( q - 1 \) . We now estimate

\[
{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell } = \left\{  {{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }}\right\}
\]

by induction on \( q \) using (4.1.8) with \( \lambda  = q \) . Noticing a total of \( q + 2 \) terms contracting \( {A}_{ij} \) with a derivative of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) of degree \( q \) , we get the estimate

\[
q\sup \left| {{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  \left( {q + 2}\right) \sup \left| A\right| \sup \left| {{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  + \sup \left| {\Psi }^{q}\right| .
\]

and everything works. This proves that there exists a constant \( c > 0 \) depending only on the dimension, and constants \( {C}_{q} \) depending only on the dimension and \( q \) and bounds \( {B}_{j} \) on the curvature and its derivatives for \( j \leq  q \) where \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {B}_{j} \) , so that for any metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) the Euclidean metric \( {I}_{k\ell } \) satisfies

\[
\frac{1}{2}{g}_{k\ell } \leq  {I}_{k\ell } \leq  2{g}_{k\ell }
\]

and the covariant derivatives of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) with respect to \( {g}_{k\ell } \) satisfy

\[
\left| {{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}.
\]

The difference between a covariant derivative and an ordinary derivative is given by the connection

\[
- {\Gamma }_{ij}^{p}{I}_{pk} - {\Gamma }_{ik}^{p}{I}_{pj}
\]

to get

\[
{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = \frac{1}{2}{I}^{k\ell }\left( {{D}_{\ell }{I}_{ij} - {D}_{i}{I}_{j\ell } - {D}_{j}{I}_{i\ell }}\right) .
\]

This gives us bounds on \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) . We then obtain bounds on the first derivatives of \( {g}_{ij} \) from

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{g}_{jk} = {g}_{k\ell }{\Gamma }_{ij}^{\ell } + {g}_{j\ell }{\Gamma }_{ik}^{\ell }.
\]

Always proceeding inductively on the order of the derivative, we now get bounds on covariant derivatives of \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) from the covariant derivatives of \( {I}_{pk} \) and bounds of the ordinary derivatives of \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) by relating the to the covariant derivatives using the \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) , and bounds on the ordinary derivatives of the \( {g}_{jk} \) from bounds on the ordinary derivatives of the \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{\ell } \) . Consequently, we have estimates

\[
\frac{1}{2}{I}_{k\ell } \leq  {g}_{k\ell } \leq  2{I}_{k\ell }
\]

and

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{1}}}\cdots \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{q}}}{g}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {\widetilde{C}}_{q}
\]

for similar constants \( {\widetilde{C}}_{q} \) .

Therefore we have finished the proof of Claim 1.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
### 2.1 Notation and conventions

Throughout this chapter, \( X, Y, W \) and \( Z \) will be fixed vector fields on a manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , and \( A \) and \( B \) will be more general tensor fields, with possibly different type. \( {}^{1} \)

We assume that \( \mathcal{M} \) is endowed with a Riemannian metric \( g \) , or a smooth family of such metrics depending on one parameter \( t \) . This metric then extends to arbitrary tensors. (See, for example, [27, Lemma 3.1].)

We will write \( \nabla \) for the Levi-Civita connection of \( g \) . Recall that it may be extended to act on arbitrary tensor fields. (See, for example [27, Lemma 4.6].) It is also important to keep in mind that the Levi-Civita connection commutes with traces, or equivalently that \( \nabla g = 0 \) , and that we have the product rule \( {\nabla }_{X}\left( {A \otimes  B}\right)  = \left( {{\nabla }_{X}A}\right)  \otimes  B + A \otimes  \left( {{\nabla }_{X}B}\right) \) . See [27, Lemma 4.6] for more on what this implies. When we apply \( \nabla \) without a subscript, we adopt the convention of seeing \( {\nabla }_{X}A = \nabla A\left( {X,\ldots }\right) \) , that is, the \( X \) appears as the first rather than the last entry. (More details, could be found in [14, (2.60)] or with the opposite convention in [27, Lemma 4.7].)

---

\( {}^{1} \) A tensor field of type \( \left( {p, q}\right) \) , with \( p, q \in  \{ 0\}  \cup  \mathbb{N} \) is a section of the tensor product of the bundles \( { \otimes  }^{p}T\mathcal{M} \) and \( { \otimes  }^{q}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) .

---

We need notation for the second covariant derivative of a tensor field, and write

\[
{\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y} - {\nabla }_{{\nabla }_{X}Y}.
\]

That way, we have

\[
{\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2}A \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}A - {\nabla }_{{\nabla }_{X}Y}A \equiv  \left( {{\nabla }^{2}A}\right) \left( {X, Y,\ldots }\right) ,
\]

where \( {\nabla }^{2}A \) is the covariant derivative of \( \nabla A \) . When applied to a function, we get the Hessian

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \nabla {df}.
\]

We adopt the sign convention

\[
{\Delta A} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\operatorname{tr}}_{12}{\nabla }^{2}A
\]

for the connection (or rough) Laplacian of \( A \) , where \( {\operatorname{tr}}_{12} \) means to trace over the first and second entries (here of \( {\nabla }^{2}A \) ).

We adopt the sign convention

(2.1.1)

\[
R\left( {X, Y}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X} - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y} + {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{Y, X}^{2} - {\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2}.
\]

for the curvature. This may be applied to any tensor field, and again satisfies the product rule \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) \left( {A \otimes  B}\right)  = \left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) A}\right)  \otimes  B + A \otimes  \left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) B}\right) \) . Of course, \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) f = 0 \) for any function \( f : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) - equivalently the Hessian Hess \( \left( f\right) \) of a function \( f \) is symmetric - but \( {\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2} \) is not otherwise symmetric in \( X \) and \( Y \) . Indeed, we have, for any tensor field \( A \in  \Gamma \left( {{ \otimes  }^{k}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right) \) , the Ricci identity

\[
- {\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2}A\left( {W, Z,\ldots }\right)  + {\nabla }_{Y, X}^{2}A\left( {W, Z,\ldots }\right)
\]

(2.1.2)

\[
\equiv  \left\lbrack  {R\left( {X, Y}\right) A}\right\rbrack  \left( {W, Z,\ldots }\right)
\]

\[
\equiv  \left\lbrack  {R\left( {X, Y}\right) A}\right\rbrack  \left( {W, Z,\ldots }\right)  - R\left( {X, Y}\right) \left\lbrack  {A\left( {W, Z,\ldots }\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\equiv   - A\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z,\ldots }\right)  - A\left( {W, R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z,\ldots }\right)  - \ldots
\]

We also may write \( {}^{2} \)

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z\rangle .
\]

---

\( {}^{2} \) We use \( g\left( {\cdot , \cdot  }\right) \) and \( \langle  \cdot  , \cdot  \rangle \) interchangeably, although with the latter, it is easier to forget any \( t \) -dependence that \( g \) might have.

---

Note that about half - perhaps more - of books adopt the opposite sign convention for \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) \) . We agree with [10],[14],[29], etc. but not with [27] etc. This way makes more sense because we then have the agreement with classical notation:

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j},{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{l}}\right)  = {R}_{ijkl}.
\]

(A few people adopt the opposite sign convention for \( {R}_{ijkl} \) .) This way round, \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) \) then serves, roughly speaking, as the infinitesimal holonomy rotation as one parallel translates around an infinitesimal anticlockwise loop in the ’plane’ \( X \land  Y \) . It also leads to a more natural definition of the curvature operator \( \mathcal{R} : { \land  }^{2}T\mathcal{M} \rightarrow  { \land  }^{2}T\mathcal{M} \) , namely

\[
\langle \mathcal{R}\left( {X \land  Y}\right) , W \land  Z\rangle  = \operatorname{Rm}\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right) . \tag{2.1.3}
\]

The various symmetries of Rm ensure that \( \mathcal{R} \) is thus well defined, and is symmetric. If \( X \) and \( Y \) are orthogonal unit vectors at some point, then the sectional curvature of the plane \( X \land  Y \) is \( {Rm}\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right) \) with our convention.

We denote the Ricci and scalar curvatures by

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Rm}\left( {X,\cdot , Y, \cdot  }\right) ,
\]

and

\[
R \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Ric},
\]

respectively. (There should not be any ambiguity about the sign of these!) Occasionally we write, say, \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right) \) or \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{g} \) to emphasise the metric we are using.

Some of the formulae which we will be requiring can be dramatically simplified, without losing relevant information, by using the following '*'-notation. We denote by \( A * B \) any tensor field which is a (real) linear combination of tensor fields, each formed by starting with the tensor field \( A \otimes  B \) , using the metric to switch the type of any number of \( {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) components to \( T\mathcal{M} \) components, or vice versa (that is, raising or lowering some indices) taking any number of contractions, and switching any number of components in the product. Here, the algorithm for arriving at a certain expression \( A * B \) must be independent of the particular choice of tensors \( A \) and \( B \) of their respective types, and hence we are free to estimate \( \left| {A * B}\right|  \leq  C\left| A\right| \left| B\right| \) for some constant \( C \) which will depend neither on \( A \) nor \( B \) . Generally, the precise dependencies of \( C \) should be clear in context, and in these notes we will typically have \( C = C\left( n\right) \) when making such an estimate.

The fact that \( g \) is parallel gives us the product rule

\[
\nabla \left( {A * B}\right)  = \left( {\nabla A}\right)  * B + A * \left( {\nabla B}\right) . \tag{2.1.4}
\]

As an example of the use of this notation, the expression \( {R}^{2} = \mathrm{{Rm}} * \mathrm{{Rm}} \) , or even \( R = \mathrm{{Rm}} * 1 \) , would be valid, albeit not very useful. The Ricci identity (2.1.2) can be weakened to the useful notational aid

\[
R\left( {\cdot , \cdot  }\right) A = A * \mathrm{{Rm}}, \tag{2.1.5}
\]

valid in this form for tensor fields \( A \) of arbitrary type. One identity which follows easily from this expression is the formula for commuting the covariant derivative and the Laplacian:

\[
\nabla \left( {\Delta A}\right)  - \Delta \left( {\nabla A}\right)  = \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}} * A + \mathrm{{Rm}} * \nabla A. \tag{2.1.6}
\]

We will be regularly using the divergence operator \( \delta  : \Gamma \left( {{ \otimes  }^{k}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right)  \rightarrow \; \Gamma \left( {{ \otimes  }^{k - 1}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right) \) defined by \( \delta \left( T\right)  =  - {\operatorname{tr}}_{12}\nabla T \) . Again, \( {\operatorname{tr}}_{12} \) means to trace over the first and second entries (here of \( \nabla T \) ).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( \left( {W, h\left( t\right) }\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , be a Ricci flow and fix \( \Theta  < \infty \) . Then there exist constants \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( 0 < {r}_{0} \leq  1 \) depending only on the curvature bound for the ambient Ricci flow and \( \Theta \) such that the following holds. Let \( c\left( {x, t}\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , be a curve-shrinking flow with \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) immersed for each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) and with the total curvature of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) \) being at most \( \Theta \) . Suppose that there is \( 0 < r \leq  {r}_{0} \) and at a time \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1} - \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) such that the length of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) is at least \( r \) and the total curvature of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) on any sub-arc of length \( r \) is at most \( \delta \) . Then for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) the curvature \( k \) satisfies

\[
{k}^{2} \leq  \frac{2}{\left( t - {t}^{\prime }\right) }.
\]

The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of this lemma. In [2] such a local estimate was established when the ambient manifold was Euclidean space and the curve in question is a graph. A related result for hypersurfaces that are graphs appears in [19]. The passage from Euclidean space to a general Ricci flow is straightforward, but it is more delicate to use the bound on total curvature on initial sub-arcs of length \( r \) to show that in appropriate coordinates the evolving curve can be written as an evolving graph, so that the analysis in [2] can be applied.

We fix \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small. We fix \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1} - \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) for which the hypotheses of the lemma hold. The strategy of the proof is to first restrict to the maximum subinterval of \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) of \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) on which \( k \) is bounded by \( \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) . If \( {t}_{2} < {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) , then \( k \) achieves the bound \( \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) at time \( {t}_{2} \) . We show that in fact on this subinterval \( k \) never achieves the bound. The result then follows. To show that \( k \) never achieves the bound, we show that on a possibly smaller interval of time \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}_{3} \leq  {t}_{2} \) we can write the restriction of the curve-shrinking flow to any interval whose length at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) is \( \left( {0.9}\right) r \) as a family of graphs in a local coordinate system so that the function \( f \) (of arc and time) defining the graph has derivative along the arc bounded in norm by \( 1/2 \) . We take \( {t}_{3} \leq  {t}_{2} \) maximal with respect to these conditions. Then with both the bound on \( k \) and the bound on the derivative of \( f \) one shows that the spatial derivative of \( f \) never reaches \( 1/2 \) and also that the curves do not move too much so that they always remain in the coordinate patch. The only way that this can happen is that if \( {t}_{2} = {t}_{3} \) , that is to say, on the entire time interval where we have the curvature bound, we also can write the curve-shrinking flow as a flow of graphs with small spatial derivatives. Then it is convenient to replace the curve-shrinking flow by an equivalent flow, introduced in [2], called the graph flow. Applying a simple maximum principle argument to this flow we see that \( k \) never achieves the value \( \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and hence the curvature estimate \( k < \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) holds throughout the interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

8.1. A bound for \( \int {kds} \) . Recall that \( k \) is the norm of the curvature vector \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) , and in particular, \( k \geq  0 \) . For any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) we let \( {\gamma }_{t} \) be the result at time \( t \) of applying the curve-shrinking flow to \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . The purpose of this subsection is to show that \( {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} \) is small for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) and all initial arcs \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length at most \( r \) .

CLAIM 19.59. There is a constant \( {D}_{0} < \infty \) , depending only on \( \Theta \) and the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow such that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) and every sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) whose length is at most \( r \) , we have \( {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} < {D}_{0} \) and \( l\left( {\gamma }_{t}\right)  \leq  {D}_{0}r \) , where \( l\left( {\gamma }_{t}\right) \) is the length of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) .

Proof. This is immediate from Corollary 19.10 applied to all of \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) .

Now we fix \( {t}_{2} \leq  {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) maximal subject to the condition that \( k\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}} \) for all \( x \) and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . If \( {t}_{2} < {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) then there is \( x \) with \( k\left( {x,{t}_{2}}\right)  = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\left( {t}_{2} - {t}^{\prime }\right) }}. \)

Now consider a curve \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) . From the integral estimate in the previous claim and the assumed pointwise estimate on \( k \) , we see that

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{k}^{2}{ds} \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  {\gamma }_{t}}}k\left( {x, t}\right) {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} < \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}} \cdot  {D}_{0}.
\]

Using Equation (19.8), it follows easily that, provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the length of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) is at least \( \left( {0.9}\right) r \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , and more generally for any subinterval \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) the length of the corresponding interval \( {\gamma }_{t}^{\prime } \) is at least (0.9) times the length of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) . We introduce a cut-off function on \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) as follows. First, fix a smooth function \( \psi  : \left\lbrack  {-1/2,1/2}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) which is identically zero on \( \left\lbrack  {-{0.50}, - {0.45}}\right\rbrack \) and on \( \left\lbrack  {{0.45},{0.50}}\right\rbrack \) , and is identically 1 on \( \left\lbrack  {-3/8,3/8}\right\rbrack \) . There is a constant \( {D}^{\prime } \) such that \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime }\right|  \leq  {D}^{\prime } \) and \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime \prime }\right|  \leq  {D}^{\prime } \) . Now we fix the midpoint \( {x}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and define the signed distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right) \) , denoted

\[
s : {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R}
\]

as follows:

\[
s\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| {dy}.
\]

We define the cut-off function

\[
\varphi \left( {x, t}\right)  = \psi \left( \frac{s\left( {x, t}\right) }{r}\right) .
\]

CLAIM 19.60. There is a constant \( {D}_{1} \) depending only on the curvature bound for the ambient Ricci flow such that for any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) , defining \( \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) \) as above, for all \( x \in  {\gamma }_{t} \) and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) we have

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}_{1}}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + {D}_{1}.
\]

Proof. Clearly,

\[
\frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t} = {\psi }^{\prime }\left( \frac{s\left( {x, t}\right) }{r}\right)  \cdot  \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}.
\]

We know that \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime }\right|  \leq  {D}^{\prime } \) so that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{r}\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right| .
\]

On the other hand,

\[
s\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| {dy}
\]

so that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  = \left| {{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\frac{\partial \left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| }{\partial t}{dy}}\right| ,
\]

By Lemma 19.6 we have

\[
\frac{\partial \left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| }{\partial y}{dy} = \left( {-\operatorname{Ric}\left( {S\left( {y, t}\right) , S\left( {y, t}\right) }\right)  - {k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) }\right) {ds},
\]

so that there is a constant \( D \) depending only on the bound of the sectional curvatures of the ambient Ricci flow with

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left( {D + {k}^{2}}\right) {ds} \leq  {Dl}\left( {\gamma }_{t}\right)  + {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right) ,
\]

and hence by Claim 19.59

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  D{D}_{0}r + {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right) .
\]

Using the fact that \( {k}^{2} \leq  2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right)  \leq  \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{kds} \leq  \frac{\sqrt{2}{D}_{0}}{\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Putting all this together, we see that there is a constant \( {D}_{1} \) such that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  {D}_{1}\left( {\frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + 1}\right) .
\]

CLAIM 19.61. There is a constant \( {D}_{2} \) depending only on the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow and \( \Theta \) and a constant \( {D}_{3} \) depending only on the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow, such that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) , we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{2}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right)  + \frac{{D}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} + {D}_{3}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}.
\]

Proof. We have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}{kds}}\right|  + \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi \frac{\partial \left( {kds}\right) }{\partial t}}\right| .
\]

Using Claim 19.60 for the first term and Claim 19.8 and arguing as in the proof of Lemma 19.9 for the second term, we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{1}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right) {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} + \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds}}\right|  + {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{C}_{1}^{\prime }{\varphi kds},
\]

where \( {C}_{1}^{\prime } \) depends only on the ambient curvature bound. We bound the first term by

\[
{D}_{1}{D}_{0}\left( {\frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + 1}\right) ,
\]

where \( {D}_{0} \) is the constant depending on \( \Theta \) and the ambient curvature bound from Claim 19.59. Since the ends of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) are at distance at least \( \left( {0.45}\right) r \) from \( {x}_{0} \) all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , we see that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime } = {\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }.
\]

Integrating by parts we have

\[
{\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds} = {\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }{\varphi }^{\prime \prime }{kds},
\]

where the prime here refers to the derivative along \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with respect to arc length. Of course \( \left| {\varphi }^{\prime \prime }\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{{r}^{2}} \) . Thus, we see that

\[
\left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds}}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{{r}^{2}}{\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }{kds} \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }{D}_{0}}{{r}^{2}}.
\]

Putting all this together, we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{2}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right)  + \frac{{D}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} + {D}_{3}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}
\]

for \( {D}_{2} = {D}_{0}\max \left( {{D}^{\prime },{D}_{1}}\right) \) and \( {D}_{3} = {C}_{1}^{\prime } \) . This gives the required estimate.

COROLLARY 19.62. For any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) we have

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds} \leq  {D}_{4}\sqrt{\delta }
\]

for a constant \( {D}_{4} \) that depends only on the sectional curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow and \( \Theta \) .

Proof. This is immediate from the previous result by integrating from \( {t}^{\prime } \) to \( {t}_{2} \leq  {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) , and using the fact that \( \delta  < 1 \) and \( r < 1 \) , and using the fact that

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}}{\varphi kds} \leq  {\int }_{{\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}}{kds} < \delta
\]

since \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) has length at most \( r \) .

This gives:

COROLLARY 19.63. For \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \subset  c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) a sub-arc of length at most \( r \) and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} \leq  2{D}_{4}\sqrt{\delta }.
\]

For any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and any sub-arc \( J \subset  c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) of length at most \( r/2 \) with respect to the metric \( h\left( t\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{J}k\left( {x, t}\right) {ds}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{D}_{4}\sqrt{\delta }.
\]

Proof. We divide an interval \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \subset  c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) of length at most \( r \) into two subintervals \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) of lengths at most \( r/2 \) . Let \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) be intervals of length \( r \) containing \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) respectively as middle subintervals. We then apply the previous corollary to \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) using the fact that \( {\varphi k} \geq  0 \) everywhere and \( {\varphi k} = k \) on the middle subintervals of \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) . For an interval \( J \subset  {\gamma }_{t} \) of length \( r/2 \) , according to Lemma 19.10 the length of \( {\left. {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\right| }_{J} \) with respect to the metric \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) is at most \( r \) , and hence this case follows from the previous case.

8.2. Writing the curve flow as a graph. Now we restrict attention to \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , the maximal interval in \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) where \( {k}^{2} \leq  2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) be an arc of length \( r \) in \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) and let \( {x}_{0} \) be the central point of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Denote \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  = p \in  W \) . We take the \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) -exponential mapping from \( {T}_{p}W \rightarrow  W \) . This map will be a local diffeomorphism out to a distance determined by the curvature of \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) . For an appropriate choice of the ball (depending on the ambient curvature bound) the metric on the ball induced by pulling back \( h\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) will be within \( \delta \) in the \( {C}^{1} \) -topology to the Euclidean metric \( {h}^{\prime } = h{\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }_{p} \) . By this we mean that

(1) \( \left| {\langle X, Y{\rangle }_{h\left( t\right) }-\langle X, Y{\rangle }_{{h}^{\prime }}}\right|  < \delta {\left| X\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}{\left| Y\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \) for all tangent vectors in the coordinate system, and

(2) viewing the connection \( \Gamma \) as a bilinear map on the coordinate space with values in the coordinate space we have \( {\left| \Gamma \left( X, Y\right) \right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} < \; \delta {\left| X\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}{\left| Y\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \)

We choose \( 0 < {r}_{0} \leq  1 \) so that it is much smaller than this distance, and hence \( r \) is also much smaller than this distance. We lift to the ball in \( {T}_{p}W \) .

We fix orthonormal coordinates with respect to the metric \( {h}^{\prime } \) so that the tangent vector of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {x}_{0}\right) \) points in the positive \( {x}^{1} \) -direction. Using these coordinates we decompose the coordinate patch as a product of an interval in the \( {x}^{1} \) -direction and an open ball, \( B \) , spanned by the remaining Euclidean coordinates. From now on we shall work in this coordinate system using this product structure. To simplify the notation in the coming computations, we rename the \( {x}^{1} \) -coordinate the \( z \) -coordinate. Ordinary derivatives of a function \( \alpha \) with respect to \( z \) are written \( {\alpha }_{z} \) . When we write norms and inner products without indicating the metric we implicitly mean that the metric is \( h\left( t\right) \) . When we use the Euclidean metric on these coordinates we denote it explicitly. Next, we wish to understand how \( {\gamma }_{t} \) moves in the Euclidean coordinates under the curve-shrinking flow. Since we have \( {\left| {\nabla }_{S}S\right| }_{h} = k \) , it follows that \( {\left| {\nabla }_{S}S\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  \sqrt{1 + \delta }k \leq  2/\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }} \) , and hence, integrating tells us that for any \( x \in  {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) we have

\[
{\left| {\gamma }_{t}\left( x\right)  - {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( x\right) \right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  4\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }} \leq  4\sqrt{\delta }r.
\]

This shows that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , the curve \( {\gamma }_{t} \) is contained in the coordinate patch that we are considering. This computation also implies that the \( z \) -coordinate of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) changes by at most \( 4\sqrt{\delta }r \) over this time interval.

Because the total curvature of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is small and the metric is close to the Euclidean metric, it follows that the tangent vector at every point of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is close to the positive \( z \) -direction. This means that we can write \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) as a graph of a function \( f \) from a subinterval in the \( z \) -line to \( Y \) with \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} < {2\delta } \) . By continuity, there is \( {t}_{3} \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) such that all the curves \( {\gamma }_{t} \) are written as graphs of functions (over subintervals of the \( z \) -axis that depend on \( t \) ) with \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) . That is to say, we have an open subset \( U \) of the product of the \( z \) -axis with \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) , and the evolving curves define a map \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) from \( U \) into the coordinate system, where the slices at constant time are graphs \( z \mapsto  \left( {z, f\left( {z, t}\right) }\right) \) and are the curves \( {\gamma }_{t} \) . Using the coordinates \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) gives a new flow of curves by moving in the \( t \) -direction. This new flow is called the graph flow. It is a reparameterization of the curve shrinking flow in such a way that the \( z \) -coordinate is preserved. We denote by \( Z = Z\left( {z, t}\right) \) the image under the differential of the map \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) of the tangent vector in the \( z \) -direction and by \( Y\left( {z, t}\right) \) the image under the differential of \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) of the tangent vector in the \( t \) -direction. Notice that \( Z \) is the tangent vector along the parameterized curves in the graph flow. Since we are now using a different parameterization of the curves from the one determined by the curve-shrinking flow, the tangent vector \( Z \) has the same direction but not necessarily the same length as the tangent vector \( X \) from the curve-shrinking parameterization. Also, notice that in the Euclidean norm we have \( {\left| Z\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2} = 1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2} \) . It follows that on \( U \) we have

\[
\left( {1 - \delta }\right) \left( {1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2}}\right)  \leq  {\left| Z\left( z, t\right) \right| }_{h\left( t\right) }^{2} \leq  \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \left( {1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2}}\right) .
\]

In particular, because of our restriction to the subset where \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) we have \( \left( {1 - \delta }\right)  \leq  {\left| Z\left( z, t\right) \right| }_{h\left( t\right) }^{2} \leq  \left( {1.01}\right) \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) .

Now we know that \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a graph of a function \( f\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) defined on some interval \( I \) along the \( z \) -axis. Let \( {I}^{\prime } \) be the subinterval of \( I \) centered in \( I \) with \( {h}^{\prime } \) -length (0.9) times the \( {h}^{\prime } \) -length of \( I \) . By the above estimate on \( \left| Z\right| \) it follows that the restriction of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) to \( {I}^{\prime } \) has length between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) , and also that the \( {h}^{\prime } \) -length of \( {I}^{\prime } \) is between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) . The above estimate means that, provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) there is a subinterval of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) that is the graph of a function defined on all of \( {I}^{\prime } \) . We now restrict attention to the family of curves parameterized by \( {I}^{\prime } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) . For every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) the curve \( {\left. {\gamma }_{t}\right| }_{{I}^{\prime }} \) has length between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) . The curve-shrinking flow is not defined on this product because under the curve-shrinking flow the \( z \) -coordinate of any given point is not constant. But the graph flow defined above, and studied in [2] (in the case of Euclidean background metric), is defined on \( {I}^{\prime } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) since this flow preserves the \( z \) -coordinate. The time partial derivative in the curve-shrinking flow is given by

(19.10)

\[
{\nabla }_{S}S = \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} - \frac{1}{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}}\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z}\right\rangle  Z.
\]

The time partial derivative in the graph-flow is given by \( Y = \partial \widetilde{\gamma }/\partial t \) . The tangent vector \( Y \) is characterized by being \( {h}^{\prime } \) -orthogonal to the \( z \) -axis and differing from \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) by a functional multiple of \( Z \) .

CLAIM 19.64.

\[
Y = \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z-\langle \Gamma \left( {Z, Z}\right) ,{\partial }_{z}{\rangle }_{{h}^{\prime }}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} = {\nabla }_{S}S + \left( {\frac{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z\right\rangle  }{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}} - \frac{{\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}}\right) Z.
\]

Proof. In our Euclidean coordinates, \( Z = \left( {1,{f}_{z}}\right) \) so that \( {\nabla }_{Z}Z = \; \left( {0,{f}_{zz}}\right)  + \Gamma \left( {Z, Z}\right) \) . Thus,

\[
{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }} = {\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}.
\]

Since \( {\left\langle  Z,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }} = 1 \) , it follows that

\[
\frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z - {\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}
\]

is \( {h}^{\prime } \) -orthogonal to the \( z \) -axis and hence is a multiple of \( Y \) . Since it differs by a multiple of \( Z \) from \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) , it follows that it is \( Y \) . This gives the first equation; the second follows from this and Equation (19.10).

To simplify the notation we set

\[
\psi \left( Z\right)  = \frac{{\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}.
\]

Notice that from the conditions on \( \Gamma \) and \( {h}^{\prime } \) it follows immediately that \( \left| {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right|  < \left( {1.5}\right) \delta . \)

8.3. Proof that \( {t}_{3} = {t}_{2} \) . At this point we have a product coordinate system on which the metric is almost the Euclidean metric in the \( {C}^{1} \) -sense, and we have the graph flow given by

\[
Y = \frac{\partial \widetilde{\gamma }}{\partial t} = \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} - \psi \left( Z\right) Z
\]

defined on \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) with image always contained in the given coordinate patch and written as a graph over a fixed interval \( {I}^{\prime } \) in the \( z \) -axis. For every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) the length of \( {\left. {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\right| }_{{I}^{\prime }} \) in the metric \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) is between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) . The function \( f\left( {z, t}\right) \) whose graphs give the flow satisfies \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) . Our next goal is to estimate \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \) and show that it is always less than \( 1/{10} \) as long as \( {k}^{2} \leq  2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( t - {t}^{\prime } \leq  \delta {r}^{2} \) for a sufficiently small \( \delta \) , i.e., for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) ; that is to say, our next goal is to prove that \( {t}_{3} = {t}_{2} \) . In all the arguments that follow \( {C}^{\prime } \) is a constant that depends only on the curvature bound for the ambient Ricci flow, but the value of \( {C}^{\prime } \) is allowed to change from line to line.

The first step in doing this is to consider the angle between \( {\nabla }_{Z}Z \) and \( Z \) .

CLAIM 19.65. Provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the angle (measured in \( h\left( t\right) ) \) between \( Y \) and \( Z = \left( {1,{f}_{z}}\right) \) is greater than \( \pi /4 \) . Also:

(1)

\[
k \leq  \left| Y\right|  < \sqrt{2}k
\]

(2)

\[
\left| \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z}\right\rangle  \right|  < \left( {k + {2\delta }}\right) {\left| Z\right| }^{3}.
\]

(3)

\[
\left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right|  < 2\left( {\left| Y\right|  + \delta }\right)
\]

(4)

\[
\left| {\langle Y, Z\rangle }\right|  \leq  \left| Y\right| \left| {f}_{z}\right| \left( {1 + {3\delta }}\right) .
\]

Proof. Under the hypothesis that \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) , it is easy to see that the Euclidean angle between \( \left( {0,{f}_{zz}}\right) \) and \( \left( {1,{f}_{z}}\right) \) is at most \( \pi /2 - \pi /5 \) . From this, the first statement follows immediately provided that \( \delta \) is sufficiently small. Since \( Y \) is the sum of \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) and a multiple of \( Z \) and since \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) is \( h\left( t\right) \) -orthogonal to \( Z \) , it follows that \( \left| Y\right|  = \left| {{\nabla }_{S}S}\right| {\left( \cos \left( \theta \right) \right) }^{-1} \) , where \( \theta \) is the angle between \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) and \( Y \) . Since \( Y \) is a multiple of \( \left( {0,{f}_{zz}}\right) \) , it follows from the first part of the claim that the \( h\left( t\right) \) -angle between \( Y \) and \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) is less than \( \pi /4 \) . Item (1) of the claim then follows from the fact that by definition \( \left| {{\nabla }_{S}S}\right|  = k. \)

Since

\[
\frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} = Y + \psi \left( Z\right) Z
\]

and \( {\left| Z\right| }^{2} \leq  \left( {1.01}\right) \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) , the third item is immediate. For item (4), since \( Y \) is \( {h}^{\prime } \) -orthogonal to the \( z \) -axis, we have

\[
\left| {\langle Y, Z{\rangle }_{{h}^{\prime }}}\right|  = \left| {\left\langle  Y,\left( 0,{f}_{z}\right) \right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}\right|  \leq  {\left| Y\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}{\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}.
\]

From this and the comparison of \( h\left( t\right) \) and \( {h}^{\prime } \) , item (4) is immediate. Lastly, let us consider item (2). We have

\[
\langle Y, Z\rangle  = \frac{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z\right\rangle  }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} - {\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}.
\]

Thus, from item (4) we have

\[
\frac{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z\right\rangle  }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} \leq  \left| Y\right| \left| {f}_{z}\right| \left( {1 + {3\delta }}\right)  + \left( {1.5}\right) \delta .
\]

Since \( Y < \sqrt{2}k \) and \( \left| {f}_{z}\right|  < 1/{10} \) , item (2) follows.

CLAIM 19.66. The following hold provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small:

(1) \( \left| {Z\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) }\right|  < {C}^{\prime }\left( {1 + \delta \left| Y\right| }\right) \) , and

(2) \( \left| {Y\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) }\right|  < {C}^{\prime }\left( {\left| Y\right|  + \delta \left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Y}\right| }\right) \) .

(Recall that \( {C}^{\prime } \) is a constant depending only on the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow.)

Proof. For the first item, we write \( Z\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) \) as a sum of terms where the differentiation by \( Z \) acts on the various. When the \( Z \) -derivative acts on \( \Gamma \) the resulting term has norm bounded by a constant depending only on the curvature of the ambient Ricci flow. When the \( Z \) -derivative acts on one of the \( Z \) -terms in \( \Gamma \left( {Z, Z}\right) \) the norm of the result is bounded by \( {2\delta }\left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right| \left| Z\right| \) . Action on each of the other \( Z \) -terms gives a term bounded in norm by the same expression. Lastly, when the \( Z \) -derivative acts on the constant metric \( {h}^{\prime } \) the norm of the result is bounded by \( 2{\delta }^{2} \) . Since \( \left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right|  \leq  2\left( {\left| Y\right|  + \delta }\right) \) , the first item follows.

We compute \( Y\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) \) in a similar fashion. When the \( Y \) -derivative acts on the \( \Gamma \) , the norm of the result is bounded by \( {C}^{\prime }\left| Y\right| \) . When the \( Y \) -derivative acts on one of the \( Z \) -terms the norm of the result is bounded by \( {2\delta }\left| {{\nabla }_{Y}Z}\right| \) . Lastly, when the \( Y \) -derivative acts on the constant metric \( {h}^{\prime } \) , the norm of the result is bounded by \( {\delta }^{2}\left| Y\right| \) . Putting all these terms together establishes the second inequality above.

Now we wish to compute \( {\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }{\left| Z\right| }^{2}{dz} \) . To do this we first note that using the definition of \( Y \) , and arguing as in the proof of the first equation in of Lemma 19.6 we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} =  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)  + 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}Z, Z}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)  + 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Y, Z}\right\rangle  .
\]

Direct computation shows that

\[
2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}\left( \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   = Z\left( \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2\frac{{\left| {\nabla }_{Z}Z\right| }^{2}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}}{\left| Z\right| }^{2}.
\]

Thus from the Claim 19.64, we have

(19.11)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} = 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Y, Z}\right\rangle   - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= Z\left( \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2\frac{{\left| {\nabla }_{Z}Z\right| }^{2}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} - 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) Z}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= Z\left( \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2{\left| Y\right| }^{2}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} + V,
\]

where

\[
V =  - 4{\left| Z\right| }^{2}\langle Y,\psi \left( Z\right) Z\rangle  - 2{\psi }^{2}\left( Z\right) {\left| Z\right| }^{4} - 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) Z}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right) .
\]

By item (1) in Claim 19.66 and item (4) in Claim 19.65 we have

(19.12)

\[
\left| V\right|  < {C}^{\prime }\left( {1 + \delta \left| Y\right| }\right)
\]

Using this and the fact that \( \left| Y\right|  \leq  \sqrt{2}k \) we compute:

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }{\left| Z\right| }^{2}{dz} \leq  {\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }Z\left( \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right) {dz} + {\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }\left( {{C}^{\prime }\left( {1 + {\delta k}}\right) }\right) {dz}
\]

\[
= {\left. \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right| }_{0}^{a} + {\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }\left( {{C}^{\prime }\left( {1 + {\delta k}}\right) }\right) {dz}
\]

\[
= {\left. 2\frac{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z\right\rangle  }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right| }_{0}^{a} + {\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }\left( {{C}^{\prime }\left( {1 + {\delta k}}\right) }\right) {dz},
\]

where we denote the endpoints of \( {I}^{\prime } \) by \( \{ 0\} \) and \( \{ a\} \) . By item (2) in Claim 19.65, the first term is at most \( 2\left( {k + {2\delta }}\right) \sqrt{\left( {1.01}\right) \left( {1 + \delta }\right) } \) , which is at most \( \frac{8}{\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} \) and the second term is at most \( {C}^{\prime }\left( {1 + {\delta k}}\right) r \) . Now integrating from \( {t}^{\prime } \) to \( t \) we see that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) we have

\[
{\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }{\left| Z\right| }^{2}{dz} \leq  {\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ {t}^{\prime }\} }{\left| Z\right| }^{2}{dz} + {16}\sqrt{\delta }r + {C}^{\prime }\delta {r}^{3} + {C}^{\prime }{\delta }^{3/2}{r}^{2}.
\]

Since \( {\left| {f}_{z}\left( z,{t}^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  {2\delta } \) and

\[
\left( {1 - \delta }\right) \left( {1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2}}\right)  \leq  {\left| Z\right| }^{2} \leq  \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \left( {1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2}}\right) ,
