The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

The following lemma is a local and space-time version of Lemma 6.1.4 on picking local (almost) maximum curvature points. We formulate it from Perelman's arguments in the section 10 of [103].

Let \( R \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( V\right) \) be an algebraic curvature tensor on \( V \) , and let \( S \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{B}\left( {V \times  {\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\right) \) be defined by (56). Then the following statements are equivalent:

(i) \( S \) has nonnegative isotropic curvature.

(ii) We have

\[
R\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3},{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{4},{e}_{1},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\mu }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda \mu R}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {1 - {\mu }^{2}}\right)  \geq  0
\]

for all orthonormal four-frames \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\}   \subset  V \) and all \( \lambda ,\mu  \in \; \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) .

(iii) We have

\[
R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  + \left| {g\left( {\zeta ,\eta }\right) g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  - g{\left( \zeta ,\eta \right) }^{2}}\right|  \geq  0
\]

for all vectors \( \zeta ,\eta  \in  {V}^{\mathbb{C}} \) .

(i) \( \Rightarrow \) (ii): Suppose that \( S \) has nonnegative isotropic curvature. Let \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) be an orthonormal four-frame in \( V \) , and let \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . We define

\[
{\widehat{e}}_{1} = \left( {{e}_{1},\left( {0,0}\right) }\right) ,\;{\widehat{e}}_{2} = \left( {\mu {e}_{2},\left( {0,\sqrt{1 - {\mu }^{2}}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
{\widehat{e}}_{3} = \left( {{e}_{3},\left( {0,0}\right) }\right) ,\;{\widehat{e}}_{4} = \left( {\lambda {e}_{4},\left( {\sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}},0}\right) }\right) .
\]

Clearly, the vectors \( \left\{  {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right\} \) form an orthonormal four-frame in \( V \times  {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . Since \( S \) has nonnegative isotropic curvature, we have

\[
S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{3}}\right)  + S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{4},{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3}}\right)  + S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{4},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2S}\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

Using (56), we obtain

\[
R\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3},{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{4},{e}_{1},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\mu }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda \mu R}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {1 - {\mu }^{2}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

(ii) \( \Rightarrow \) (iii): We next assume that (ii) holds. Let \( \zeta ,\eta  \in  {V}^{\mathbb{C}} \) be two linearly independent vectors. Moreover, we denote by \( \sigma  \subset  {V}^{\mathbb{C}} \) the complex two-plane spanned by \( \zeta ,\eta \) . By Proposition B.3, we can find an orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\}   \subset  V \) and real numbers \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) such that \( {e}_{1} + \; {i\mu }{e}_{2} \in  \sigma \) and \( {e}_{3} + {i\lambda }{e}_{4} \in  \sigma \) . For abbreviation, let \( z = {e}_{1} + {i\mu }{e}_{2} \) and \( w = {e}_{3} + {i\lambda }{e}_{4} \) . Since \( z, w \in  \sigma \) , we can find complex numbers \( a, b, c, d \) such that \( \zeta  = {az} + {bw} \) and \( \eta  = {cz} + {dw} \) . This implies

\[
R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  = {\left| ad - bc\right| }^{2}R\left( {z, w,\bar{z},\bar{w}}\right)
\]

and

\[
g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right) g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  - g{\left( \zeta ,\eta \right) }^{2} = {\left( ad - bc\right) }^{2}\left( {g\left( {z, z}\right) g\left( {w, w}\right)  - g{\left( z, w\right) }^{2}}\right) .
\]

Putting these facts together, we obtain

\[
R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  + \left| {g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right) g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  - g{\left( \zeta ,\eta \right) }^{2}}\right|
\]

\[
= {\left| ad - bc\right| }^{2}\left\lbrack  {R\left( {z, w,\bar{z},\bar{w}}\right)  + \left| {g\left( {z, z}\right) g\left( {w, w}\right)  - g{\left( z, w\right) }^{2}}\right| }\right\rbrack  .
\]

Moreover, it follows from the first Bianchi identity that

\[
R\left( {z, w,\bar{z},\bar{w}}\right)  + \left| {g\left( {z, z}\right) g\left( {w, w}\right)  - g{\left( z, w\right) }^{2}}\right|
\]

\[
= R\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3},{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{4},{e}_{1},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\mu }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda \mu R}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {1 - {\mu }^{2}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

Thus, we conclude that

\[
R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  + \left| {g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right) g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  - g{\left( \zeta ,\eta \right) }^{2}}\right|  \geq  0,
\]

as claimed.

(iii) \( \Rightarrow \) (i): We now assume that (iii) holds. We claim that \( S \) has nonnegative isotropic curvature. Let \( \left\{  {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right\} \) be an orthonormal four-frame in \( V \times  {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . We write \( {\widehat{e}}_{j} = \left( {{v}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right) \) , where \( {v}_{j} \in  V \) and \( {y}_{j} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . Moreover, we define \( \zeta  = {v}_{1} + i{v}_{2} \in  {V}^{\mathbb{C}} \) and \( \eta  = {v}_{3} + i{v}_{4} \in  {V}^{\mathbb{C}} \) . Note that

\[
R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  = R\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{1},{v}_{3}}\right)  + R\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{4},{v}_{1},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ R\left( {{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}\right)  + R\left( {{v}_{2},{v}_{4},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2R}\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

by the first Bianchi identity. Since \( \left\{  {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right\} \) is an orthonormal four-frame, we have \( \left\langle  {{v}_{k},{v}_{l}}\right\rangle   = {\delta }_{kl} - \left\langle  {{y}_{k},{y}_{l}}\right\rangle \) for all \( k, l \in  \{ 1,2,3,4\} \) . This implies

\[
g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right)  = {\left| {v}_{1}\right| }^{2} - {\left| {v}_{2}\right| }^{2} + {2i}\left\langle  {{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - {\left| {y}_{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {y}_{2}\right| }^{2} - {2i}\left\langle  {{y}_{1},{y}_{2}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - g\left( {{y}_{1} + i{y}_{2},{y}_{1} + i{y}_{2}}\right) ,
\]

\[
g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  = {\left| {v}_{3}\right| }^{2} - {\left| {v}_{4}\right| }^{2} + {2i}\left\langle  {{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - {\left| {y}_{3}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {y}_{4}\right| }^{2} - {2i}\left\langle  {{y}_{3},{y}_{4}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - g\left( {{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4},{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4}}\right) ,
\]

and

\[
g\left( {\zeta ,\eta }\right)  = \left\langle  {{v}_{1},{v}_{3}}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}\right\rangle   + i\left\langle  {{v}_{1},{v}_{4}}\right\rangle   + i\left\langle  {{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - \left\langle  {{y}_{1},{y}_{3}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{y}_{2},{y}_{4}}\right\rangle   - i\left\langle  {{y}_{1},{y}_{4}}\right\rangle   - i\left\langle  {{y}_{2},{y}_{3}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - g\left( {{y}_{1} + i{y}_{2},{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4}}\right) .
\]

Using Proposition B.1, we obtain

\[
\left| {g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right) g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  - g{\left( \zeta ,\eta \right) }^{2}}\right|
\]

\[
= \left| {g\left( {{y}_{1} + i{y}_{2},{y}_{1} + i{y}_{2}}\right) g\left( {{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4},{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4}}\right)  - g{\left( {y}_{1} + i{y}_{2},{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4}\right) }^{2}}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  g\left( {{y}_{1} + i{y}_{2},{y}_{1} - i{y}_{2}}\right) g\left( {{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4},{y}_{3} - i{y}_{4}}\right)  - {\left| g\left( {y}_{1} + i{y}_{2},{y}_{3} - i{y}_{4}\right) \right| }^{2}
\]

\[
= \left( {{\left| {y}_{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {y}_{2}\right| }^{2}}\right) \left( {{\left| {y}_{3}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {y}_{4}\right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
- {\left( \left\langle  {y}_{1},{y}_{3}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {y}_{2},{y}_{4}\right\rangle  \right) }^{2} - {\left( \left\langle  {y}_{1},{y}_{4}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {y}_{2},{y}_{3}\right\rangle  \right) }^{2}.
\]

Putting these facts together, we obtain

\[
0 \leq  R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  + \left| {g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right) g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  - g{\left( \zeta ,\eta \right) }^{2}}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  R\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{1},{v}_{3}}\right)  + R\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{4},{v}_{1},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ R\left( {{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}\right)  + R\left( {{v}_{2},{v}_{4},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2R}\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}\right)  + \left( {{\left| {y}_{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {y}_{2}\right| }^{2}}\right) \left( {{\left| {y}_{3}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {y}_{4}\right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
- {\left( \left\langle  {y}_{1},{y}_{3}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {y}_{2},{y}_{4}\right\rangle  \right) }^{2} - {\left( \left\langle  {y}_{1},{y}_{4}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {y}_{2},{y}_{3}\right\rangle  \right) }^{2}.
\]

Using (56), we conclude that

\[
S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{3}}\right)  + S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{4},{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3}}\right)  + S\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{4},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2S}\left( {{\widehat{e}}_{1},{\widehat{e}}_{2},{\widehat{e}}_{3},{\widehat{e}}_{4}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

Therefore, \( S \) has nonnegative isotropic curvature, as claimed.

\]

\[
+ R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}R\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda R}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

Putting these facts together, we conclude that \( R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  \geq  0 \) .

(iii) \( \Rightarrow \) (i): We now assume that (iii) holds. We claim that \( \widetilde{R} \) has nonnegative isotropic curvature. We write \( {\widetilde{e}}_{j} = \left( {{v}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right) \) , where \( {v}_{j} \in  V \) and \( {y}_{j} \in  \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, we define \( \zeta  = {v}_{1} + i{v}_{2} \in  {V}^{\mathbb{C}} \) and \( \eta  = {v}_{3} + i{v}_{4} \in  {V}^{\mathbb{C}} \) . \[
g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right)  = {\left| {v}_{1}\right| }^{2} - {\left| {v}_{2}\right| }^{2} + {2i}\left\langle  {{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - {y}_{1}^{2} + {y}_{2}^{2} - {2i}{y}_{1}{y}_{2}
\]

\[
=  - {\left( {y}_{1} + i{y}_{2}\right) }^{2},
\]

\[

\]

\[
=  - {y}_{3}^{2} + {y}_{4}^{2} - {2i}{y}_{3}{y}_{4}
\]

\[
=  - {\left( {y}_{3} + i{y}_{4}\right) }^{2},
\]

and

\[
g\left( {\zeta ,\eta }\right)  = \left\langle  {{v}_{1},{v}_{3}}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}\right\rangle   + i\left\langle  {{v}_{1},{v}_{4}}\right\rangle   + i\left\langle  {{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - {y}_{1}{y}_{3} + {y}_{2}{y}_{4} - i{y}_{1}{y}_{4} - i{y}_{2}{y}_{3}
\]

\[
=  - \left( {{y}_{1} + i{y}_{2}}\right) \left( {{y}_{3} + i{y}_{4}}\right) \text{ . }
\]

\[
g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right) g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  - g{\left( \zeta ,\eta \right) }^{2} = 0.
\]

\[
0 \leq  R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  = R\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{3},{v}_{1},{v}_{3}}\right)  + R\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{4},{v}_{1},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ R\left( {{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}\right)  + R\left( {{v}_{2},{v}_{4},{v}_{2},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2R}\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}\right)
\]

This implies

\[

\]

\[
+ \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{e}}_{2},{\widetilde{e}}_{3},{\widetilde{e}}_{2},{\widetilde{e}}_{3}}\right)  + \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{e}}_{2},{\widetilde{e}}_{4},{\widetilde{e}}_{2},{\widetilde{e}}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- 2\widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{e}}_{1},{\widetilde{e}}_{2},{\widetilde{e}}_{3},{\widetilde{e}}_{4}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

\]

\[

\]

Consequently, the four-frame \( \{ Z,{JZ}, W, - {JW}\} \) has zero isotropic curvature. Thus, we conclude that \( R\left( {Z,{JZ}, W,{JW}}\right)  = 0 \) , as claimed.

In the next step, we apply the identity (91) to the vectors \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left( {Z + W}\right) \) and \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left( {Z - W}\right) \) . This yields

\[

\[

\]

(93)

\]

(94)

\[

\[

\]

+ {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{\left( {S}^{\# }\right) }_{2424} + {2\lambda \mu }{\left( {S}^{\# }\right) }_{1342} + {2\lambda \mu }{\left( {S}^{\# }\right) }_{1423} \geq  0.

\[
Q{\left( S\right) }_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{1414} + {\mu }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{2424}
\]

\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {{S}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{1414} + {\mu }^{2}{S}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{S}_{2424} - {2\lambda \mu }{S}_{1234}}\right.

\left. {+\left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {1 - {\mu }^{2}}\right) f\left( \text{ scal }\right) }\right)
\]

\[

\]

and the right-hand side is positive in view of our choice of \( f \) . This shows that the family of sets \( \left\{  {{\mathcal{F}}_{t} : t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) is invariant under the Hamilton ODE.

If \( R \in  {\mathcal{F}}_{t} \) and \( S = R + {2g} \) (scal) id \( \oslash \) id, then \( S + {2f} \) (scal) id \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC2 (cf. \]

\[
+ \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {1 - {\mu }^{2}}\right) f\left( \text{ scal }\right)  \geq  0
\]

for \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . This ensures that \( \mathcal{K} \subset  {\mathcal{F}}_{0} \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Roundness). For any \( 0 < \beta  < B < \infty \) and \( \gamma  > 0 \) (however small) there exists \( M = M\left( {\beta , B,\gamma }\right)  < \infty \) such that whenever \( g\left( t\right) \) is

a Ricci flow on a closed, three-dimensional manifold, for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , with \( {\beta g}\left( 0\right)  \leq  \operatorname{Ric}\left( {g\left( 0\right) }\right)  \leq  {Bg}\left( 0\right) \) , we have

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg}}\right|  \leq  {\gamma R} + M
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
At \( t = 0 \) , we have \( \operatorname{Ric} \geq  {\beta g} > 0 \) . In terms of the eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{i} \) , this may be phrased

\[
{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  \beta  > 0
\]

We define a first convex parallel function to be

\[
{\Psi }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \beta  - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)
\]

which will be weakly negative at \( t = 0 \) . We also see readily that the weak negativity of \( {\Psi }_{1} \) is preserved under the ODE (9.7.1).

Returning to \( t = 0 \) , combining the facts \( {\beta g} \leq \) Ric and \( R \leq  {3B} \) tells us that Ric \( \geq  \frac{\beta }{3B}{Rg} \) . After defining \( \varepsilon  = \frac{\beta }{3B} \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{3}}\right) \) , and \( \delta  = \frac{2\varepsilon }{1 - {2\varepsilon }} \in  \left( {0,2}\right) \) , we know from the proof of Theorem 9.7.5 that this condition is equivalent to

\[
{\Psi }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \leq  0, \tag{9.7.6}
\]

and is also preserved under the ODE (9.7.1).

Set \( \theta  = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta } \in  \left( {\frac{1}{2},1}\right) \) . Note that at \( t = 0,{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} + \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = \; {\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  \leq  B \) and \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{3},{e}_{3}}\right)  \geq  \beta \) . Hence, by choosing \( A > 0 \) sufficiently large (depending on \( \beta \) and \( B \) ) we have

\[
{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }, \tag{9.7.7}
\]

at \( t = 0 \) .

We claim that (9.7.7) is preserved under our Ricci flow. If this were true, then by Remark 9.7.9 we would have

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg}}\right|  \leq  {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta } \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}\right) }^{\theta } = \widetilde{A}{R}^{\theta }
\]

for \( \widetilde{A} = \widetilde{A}\left( {\beta , B}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} A{2}^{-\theta } \) . The theorem would then hold with

\[
M = M\left( {\gamma ,\beta , B}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{R \geq  0}}\left( {\widetilde{A}{R}^{\theta } - {\gamma R}}\right)  < \infty .
\]

It remains to show that (9.7.7) is preserved under this Ricci flow. By Lemma 9.7.2, \( {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \) is convex, \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \) is concave and \( {\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta } \) is concave where \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  0 \) . Therefore,

\[
{\Psi }_{3} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  - A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }
\]

is a convex function where \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  0 \) , and in particular, where \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) .

We apply Theorem 9.6.1 in the situation described in Remark 9.7.1, with \( X \) consisting of all points where \( {\Psi }_{1},{\Psi }_{2} \) and \( {\Psi }_{3} \) are all weakly negative. The theorem tells us that the set \( X \) is preserved under the Ricci flow (and in particular that (9.7.7) will continue to hold) provided that \( X \) is preserved under the analogous ODE (9.6.1), or equivalently (9.7.1).

We have already remarked that both the conditions \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) and \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) are preserved under the ODE (9.7.1). We will conclude by showing that if our eigenvalues solve (9.7.1) and satisfy \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) and \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) , then whenever \( {\Psi }_{3} \geq  0 \) , the ratio \( \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }} \) is decreasing in time.

In this case, our eigenvalues satisfy \( {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} > 0 \) and \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} > 0 \) , and we may calculate that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  = \frac{2}{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2} - {\lambda }_{1}^{2} - {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)  = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)
\]

and that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = \frac{2}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2\left\lbrack  {{\lambda }_{3} + \frac{{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}}\right\rbrack   = 2\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  + \frac{2{\lambda }_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Now \( \delta {\lambda }_{3} \leq  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \) (since \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) ) and \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{2} \) , so

\[
\delta \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  \leq  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} = \frac{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}} \leq  \frac{{\left( 2{\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \geq  2\left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right) .
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left\lbrack  \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }}\right\rbrack   \leq  2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  - {2\theta }\left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right) \left( {1 - \theta \left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= 0
\]

by definition of \( \theta \) . Therefore, \( \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }} \) is decreasing as claimed, and (9.7.7) is preserved.

knowledge_statements.title: Hamilton–Ivey Curvature Pinching Estimate
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hamilton–Ivey Curvature Pinching Estimate
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Hamilton [63], Ivey [73]). Suppose we have a solution to the Ricci flow on a three-manifold which is complete with bounded curvature for each \( t \geq  0 \) . Assume at \( t = 0 \) the eigenvalues \( \lambda  \geq  \mu  \geq  \nu \) of the curvature operator at each point are bounded below by \( \nu  \geq   - 1 \) . The scalar curvature \( R = \lambda  + \mu  + \nu \) is their sum. Then at all points and all times \( t \geq  0 \) we have the pinching estimate

\[
R \geq  \left( {-\nu }\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack
\]

whenever \( \nu  < 0 \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Consider the function

\[
y = f\left( x\right)  = x\left( {\log x - 3}\right)
\]

defined on \( {e}^{2} \leq  x <  + \infty \) . It is easy to check that \( f \) is increasing and convex with range \( - {e}^{2} \leq  y <  + \infty \) . Let \( {f}^{-1}\left( y\right)  = x \) be the inverse function, which is also increasing but concave and satisfies

(2.4.3)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{y \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{{f}^{-1}\left( y\right) }{y} = 0
\]

Consider also the set \( K \) of matrices \( {M}_{\alpha \beta } \) defined by the inequalities

(2.4.4)

\[
K : \left\{  \begin{array}{l} \lambda  + \mu  + \nu  \geq   - 3, \\  \nu  + {f}^{-1}\left( {\lambda  + \mu  + \nu }\right)  \geq  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

By Theorem 2.3.1 and the assumptions in Theorem 2.4.1 at \( t = 0 \) , we only need to check that the set \( K \) defined above is closed, convex and preserved by the ODE (2.4.2).

Clearly \( K \) is closed because \( {f}^{-1} \) is continuous. \( \lambda  + \mu  + \nu \) is just the trace function of \( 3 \times  3 \) matrices which is a linear function. Hence the first inequality in (2.4.4) defines a linear half-space, which is convex. The function \( \nu \) is the least eigenvalue function, which is concave. Also note that \( {f}^{-1} \) is concave. Thus the second inequality in (2.4.4) defines a convex set as well. Therefore we proved \( K \) is closed and convex.

Under the ODE (2.4.2)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\lambda  + \mu  + \nu }\right)  = {\lambda }^{2} + {\mu }^{2} + {\nu }^{2} + {\lambda \mu } + {\lambda \nu } + {\mu \nu }
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {{\left( \lambda  + \mu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \lambda  + \nu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{2}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\geq  0\text{ . }
\]

Thus the first inequality in (2.4.4) is preserved by the ODE.

The second inequality in (2.4.4) can be written as

\[
\lambda  + \mu  + \nu  \geq  f\left( {-\nu }\right) ,\;\text{ whenever }\nu  \leq   - {e}^{2},
\]

which becomes

(2.4.5)

\[
\lambda  + \mu  \geq  \left( {-\nu }\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 2}\right\rbrack  ,\;\text{ whenever }\nu  \leq   - {e}^{2}.
\]

To show the inequality is preserved we only need to look at points on the boundary of the set. If \( \nu  + {f}^{-1}\left( {\lambda  + \mu  + \nu }\right)  = 0 \) then \( \nu  =  - {f}^{-1}\left( {\lambda  + \mu  + \nu }\right)  \leq   - {e}^{2} \) since \( {f}^{-1}\left( y\right)  \geq  {e}^{2} \) . Hence the RHS of (2.4.5) is nonnegative. We thus have \( \lambda  \geq  0 \) because \( \lambda  \geq  \mu \) . But \( \mu \) may have either sign. We split our consideration into two cases:

Case (i): \( \mu  \geq  0 \) .

We need to verify

\[
\frac{d\lambda }{dt} + \frac{d\mu }{dt} \geq  \left( {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 1}\right) \frac{d\left( {-\nu }\right) }{dt}
\]

when \( \lambda  + \mu  = \left( {-\nu }\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 2}\right\rbrack \) . Solving for

\[
\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 2 = \frac{\lambda  + \mu }{\left( -\nu \right) }
\]

and substituting above, we must show

\[
{\lambda }^{2} + {\mu \nu } + {\mu }^{2} + {\lambda \nu } \geq  \left( {\frac{\lambda  + \mu }{\left( -\nu \right) } + 1}\right) \left( {-{\nu }^{2} - {\lambda \mu }}\right)
\]

which is equivalent to

\[
\left( {{\lambda }^{2} + {\mu }^{2}}\right) \left( {-\nu }\right)  + {\lambda \mu }\left( {\lambda  + \mu  + \left( {-\nu }\right) }\right)  + {\left( -\nu \right) }^{3} \geq  0.
\]

Since \( \lambda ,\mu \) and \( \left( {-\nu }\right) \) are all nonnegative we are done in the first case.

Case (ii): \( \mu  < 0 \) .

We need to verify

\[
\frac{d\lambda }{dt} \geq  \frac{d\left( {-\mu }\right) }{dt} + \left( {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 1}\right) \frac{d\left( {-\nu }\right) }{dt}
\]

when \( \lambda  = \left( {-\mu }\right)  + \left( {-\nu }\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 2}\right\rbrack \) . Solving for

\[
\log \left( {-\nu }\right)  - 2 = \frac{\lambda  - \left( {-\mu }\right) }{\left( -\nu \right) }
\]

and substituting above, we need to show

\[
{\lambda }^{2} + {\mu \nu } \geq   - {\mu }^{2} - {\lambda \nu } + \left( {\frac{\lambda  - \left( {-\mu }\right) }{\left( -\nu \right) } + 1}\right) \left( {-{\nu }^{2} - {\lambda \mu }}\right)
\]

or

\[
{\lambda }^{2} + \left( {-\mu }\right) \left( {-\nu }\right)  \geq  \lambda \left( {-\nu }\right)  - {\left( -\mu \right) }^{2} + \left( {\frac{\lambda  - \left( {-\mu }\right) }{\left( -\nu \right) } + 1}\right) \left( {\lambda \left( {-\mu }\right)  - {\left( -\nu \right) }^{2}}\right)
\]

which reduces to

\[
{\lambda }^{2}\left( {-\nu }\right)  + \lambda {\left( -\mu \right) }^{2} + {\left( -\mu \right) }^{2}\left( {-\nu }\right)  + {\left( -\nu \right) }^{3} \geq  {\lambda }^{2}\left( {-\mu }\right)  + \lambda \left( {-\mu }\right) \left( {-\nu }\right)
\]

or equivalently

\[
\left( {{\lambda }^{2} - \lambda \left( {-\mu }\right)  + {\left( -\mu \right) }^{2}}\right) \left( {\left( {-\nu }\right)  - \left( {-\mu }\right) }\right)  + {\left( -\mu \right) }^{3} + {\left( -\nu \right) }^{3} \geq  0.
\]

Since \( {\lambda }^{2} - \lambda \left( {-\mu }\right)  + {\left( -\mu \right) }^{2} \geq  0 \) and \( \left( {-\nu }\right)  - \left( {-\mu }\right)  \geq  0 \) we are also done in the second case.

Therefore the proof is completed. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( S \) be an algebraic curvature tensor, and let \( H \) be a symmetric bilinear form on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) such that

\[
Z \mathrel{\text{ := }} {S}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{1414} + {S}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{S}_{1234} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right)  \geq  0
\]

for every orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and every \( \lambda  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, suppose that \( Z = 0 \) for one particular orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and one particular \( \lambda  \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) . Then

\[
Q{\left( S\right) }_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{1414} + Q{\left( S\right) }_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{2424} - {2\lambda Q}{\left( S\right) }_{1234}
\]

\[
+ {\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{1414}
\]

\[
+ {\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{2424}
\]

\[
- {2\lambda }{\left( H \oslash  H\right) }_{1234}
\]

\[
+ 2\left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {{\left( S * H\right) }_{11} + {\left( S * H\right) }_{22}}\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preservation of Ricci Pinching in Three Dimensions
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For all \( \varepsilon  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{3}}\right) \) and any Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) on a three-dimensional, closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , the "pinching condition"

\[
\operatorname{Ric} \geq  {\varepsilon Rg} \tag{9.7.2}
\]

is preserved.

Refer back to Remark 5.3.3 for the definition of such inequalities, if necessary.

The significance of the permitted range of values for \( \varepsilon \) is that (9.7.2) then implies \( R \geq  0 \) , and hence that \( \operatorname{Ric} \geq  0 \) , by tracing.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The eigenvalues of Ric are (in increasing order)

\[
{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2},\;{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{3},\;{\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3},
\]

and in particular, \( R = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}}\right) \) . Define \( \delta  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{2\varepsilon }{1 - {2\varepsilon }} \in  \lbrack 0,2) \) . Therefore

\[
\operatorname{Ric} \geq  {\varepsilon Rg} \Leftrightarrow  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  \varepsilon \left( {2\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\Leftrightarrow  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  \frac{2\varepsilon }{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{\lambda }_{3}
\]

\[
\Leftrightarrow  \delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \leq  0\text{ . }
\]

By Lemma 9.7.2, \( {\lambda }_{3} \) and \( \left( {-{\lambda }_{1} - {\lambda }_{2} - {\lambda }_{3}}\right) \) are convex, and thus \( \left\lbrack  {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack \) is convex.

We apply Theorem 9.6.1 in the situation described in Remark 9.7.1, with \( X \) the 0 -sublevel set of the convex function \( \Psi \left( e\right)  = \left\lbrack  {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack  \left( e\right) \) . The theorem tells us that the condition \( \left\lbrack  {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack   \leq  0 \) is preserved under the Ricci flow (and hence that Ric \( \geq  {\varepsilon Rg} \) is preserved, as desired) provided that the same condition is preserved under the analogous ODE (9.6.1), or equivalently (9.7.1). Therefore, keeping in mind Remark 9.6.2, we must simply prove that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right)  \equiv  {2\delta }\left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2}}\right)  - 2\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right) \tag{9.7.3}
\]

\[
\leq  0,
\]

whenever

\[
\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = 0. \tag{9.7.4}
\]

In this regard, note that (9.7.4) implies that both \( {\lambda }_{3} \geq  0 \) and \( \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \geq  0 \) , since \( \delta  \in  \lbrack 0,2) \) and \( {\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2} \leq  {\lambda }_{3} \) . Neglecting the easy case in which \( {\lambda }_{3} = 0 \) , (9.7.4) then implies that

\[
\delta \left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2}}\right)  - \left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{{\lambda }_{3}}\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2}}\right)  - {\lambda }_{3}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{{\lambda }_{3}}\left\lbrack  {{\lambda }_{1}^{2}{\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}{\lambda }_{1} - {\lambda }_{3}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{{\lambda }_{3}}\left\lbrack  {{\lambda }_{1}^{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{3}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= 0
\]

and hence (9.7.3) is satisfied.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If an algebraic curvature operator \( \mathbf{R} \) is 2-nonnegative, then we have the following.

(i) If we order the eigenvalues of \( \mathbf{R} \) so that \( {\mu }_{1} \leq  \cdots  \leq  {\mu }_{N} \) , then the eigenvalues \( {\mu }_{\beta } \) are nonnegative for \( \beta  \geq  2 \) and

(11.91)

\[
{\mu }_{1} \geq   - {\mu }_{2} \geq   - \frac{\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }{N - 2} =  - \frac{2\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }{n\left( {n - 1}\right)  - 4}.
\]

(ii) The scalar curvature \( \operatorname{Scal}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is nonnegative, with equality if and only if \( \mathbf{R} = 0 \) .

(iii) The Ricci curvature \( \operatorname{Rc}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is nonnegative.

Moreover, the cone \( \mathfrak{C} \) of 2-nonnegative curvature operators contains the cone of geometrically nonnegative operators.

Since \( \mathbf{R} \) is 2-nonnegative, \( {\mu }_{\alpha } + {\mu }_{\beta } \geq  0 \) for any \( \alpha  \neq  \beta \) . Hence \( {\mu }_{\alpha } \geq  0 \) for \( \alpha  \geq  2 \) and the only possible negative eigenvalue is \( {\mu }_{1} \) . Since

\[
\operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\alpha  = 1}}^{N}{\mu }_{\alpha } \geq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\alpha  \geq  3}}{\mu }_{\alpha } \geq  \left( {N - 2}\right) {\mu }_{3},
\]

formula (11.91) follows.

(ii) Let \( {\left\{  {\omega }_{\alpha }\right\}  }_{\alpha  = 1}^{N} \Doteq  {\left\{  {e}_{i} \land  {e}_{j}\right\}  }_{i < j} \) be an orthonormal basis for \( \mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) \) , where each \( \alpha \) corresponds to a pair \( \left( {i, j}\right) \) with \( i < j \) . From definition (11.39) we have

\[
\operatorname{Scal}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{\mathbf{R}}_{ijij} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{\mathbf{R}}_{\alpha \alpha }.
\]

On the other hand, since \( \mathbf{R} \) is 2-nonnegative,

\[
0 \leq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\alpha  \neq  \beta }}\left( {{\mathbf{R}}_{\alpha \alpha } + {\mathbf{R}}_{\beta \beta }}\right)  = \left( {N - 1}\right) \operatorname{Scal}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) .
\]

Hence, if \( \operatorname{Scal}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = 0 \) , then \( {\mathbf{R}}_{\alpha \alpha } + {\mathbf{R}}_{\beta \beta } = 0 \) for all pairs \( \left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \) with \( \alpha  \neq  \beta \) , which implies that \( {\mathbf{R}}_{\alpha \alpha } = 0 \) for all \( \alpha \) , i.e., \( \mathbf{R} = 0 \) .

(iii) From definition (11.38) we have

\[
\operatorname{Rc}{\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }_{ii} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k \neq  i}}\left\langle  {\mathbf{R}\left( {{e}_{i} \land  {e}_{k}}\right) ,{e}_{i} \land  {e}_{k}}\right\rangle   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\beta  \in  \mathcal{B}}}\left\langle  {\mathbf{R}\left( {\omega }_{\beta }\right) ,{\omega }_{\beta }}\right\rangle  ,
\]

where

\[
\mathcal{B} \Doteq  \{ \left( {1, i}\right) ,\left( {2, i}\right) ,\ldots ,\left( {i - 1, i}\right) ,\left( {i, i + 1}\right) ,\left( {i, i + 2}\right) ,\ldots ,\left( {i, n}\right) \} .
\]

---

\[
\omega  = \left( {y + {c}_{2}{e}_{1}}\right)  \land  \left( {z - {c}_{1}{e}_{1}}\right)  \Doteq  v \land  w.
\]

---

Since \( \mathbf{R} \) is 2-nonnegative, \( {\mathbf{R}}_{\alpha \alpha } + {\mathbf{R}}_{\beta \beta } \geq  0 \) for any \( \alpha  \neq  \beta \) and \( {\mathbf{R}}_{\gamma \gamma } < 0 \) for at most one \( \gamma  \in  \{ 1,\ldots , N\} \) . This is enough to conclude that \( \operatorname{Rc}{\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }_{ii} \geq  0 \) for any orthonormal basis \( {\left\{  {e}_{j}\right\}  }_{j = 1}^{n} \) . In fact,

\[
\operatorname{Rc}{\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }_{ii} \geq  \mathop{\inf }\limits_{\left\{  {\eta }_{k}\right\}  }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{{n - 1}}\left\langle  {\mathbf{R}\left( {\eta }_{k}\right) ,{\eta }_{k}}\right\rangle   \geq  {\mu }_{1} + {\mu }_{2} + \cdots  + {\mu }_{n - 1},
\]

where the infimum on the right-hand side is taken over all orthonormal bases \( {\left\{  {\eta }_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 1}^{n - 1} \) for \( \operatorname{span}\left\{  {{\omega }_{\beta } : \beta  \in  \mathcal{B}}\right\} \) and where \( {\mu }_{1} \leq  {\mu }_{2} \leq  \cdots  \leq  {\mu }_{N} \) are the ordered eigenvalues of \( \mathbf{R} \) . Hence we have

(11.92)

\[
\operatorname{Rc}{\left( \mathbf{R}\right) }_{ii} \geq  \left( {n - 3}\right) {\mu }_{3} \geq  \left( {n - 3}\right) \left| {\mu }_{1}\right| ,
\]

which completes the proof of (iii).

Finally, the last statement in the lemma is clear since the cone of nonnegative curvature operators contains the cone of geometrically nonnegative operators.

Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. Suppose \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) with \( T > 0 \) , is a nonflat ancient solution of the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. Then the asymptotic volume ratio of the solution metric satisfies

\[
{\nu }_{M}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{r \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {O, r}\right) }\right) }{{r}^{n}} = 0
\]

for each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) .

The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

The following lemma is a local and space-time version of Lemma 6.1.4 on picking local (almost) maximum curvature points. We formulate it from Perelman's arguments in the section 10 of [103].

Let \( C \subset  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) be a closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset which is invariant under the ordinary differential equation (1). Suppose that \( C \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) is contained in the half space of curvature operators with positive scalar curvature, that each \( \mathrm{R} \in  C \) has nonnegative Ricci curvature and that \( C \) contains all nonnegative curvature operators of rank 1 . Then for \( n \geq  3 \) and

\[
b \in  \left( {0,\frac{\sqrt{{2n}\left( {n - 2}\right)  + 4} - 2}{n\left( {n - 2}\right) }}\right\rbrack  \;\text{ and }\;{2a} = {2b} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}
\]

the set \( {\mathrm{l}}_{a, b}\left( C\right) \) is invariant under the vector field corresponding to (1) as well. In fact, it is transverse to the boundary of the set at all boundary points \( \mathrm{R} \neq  0 \) .

Using the Bianchi identity it is straightforward to check that a nonnegative curvature operator of rank 1 corresponds up to a positive factor and a change of basis in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) to the curvature operator of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  {\mathbb{R}}^{n - 2} \) . The condition that \( C \) contains all these operators is equivalent to saying that \( C \) contains the cone of geometrically nonnegative curvature operators. A curvature operator is geometrically nonnegative if it can be written as the sum of nonnegative curvature operators of rank 1. In dimensions above 4 this cone is strictly smaller than the cone of nonnegative curvature operators. Although we will not need it, we remark that the cone of geometrically nonnegative curvature operators is invariant under (1) as well.

(ii) This follows easily from (i), which shows that each of the terms in (11.66) is geometrically nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \( C < \infty \) the following holds. Suppose that \( X \) is a connected subset of a Riemannian three-manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) . Suppose that every point of \( X \) is either the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck or is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Then one of the following holds (see FIG. 4):

(1) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is the union of two \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps and is diffeomorphic to one of \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(2) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is a double \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube. This component is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(3) \( X \) is contained in a single \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

(4) \( X \) is contained in a \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(5) \( X \) is contained in an \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(6) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration, which itself is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks.
