As a consequence of the standard regularity result of elliptic partial differential equations (see for example [48]), the map \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right)  \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) \) and then from (5.3.10) we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } \leq  \delta .
\]

If \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta \) , we then finish the proof of the claim. So we may assume that \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( \omega \right) {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \delta \) . We want to show that \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) can be extended forward in time a little.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then we consider the new sequence of the manifolds \( M \) with metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) and the origins \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) . Since \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) are close to isometries, the injectivity radii of the metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \) at \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) do not go to zero, and we can extract a subsequence which converges to a hyperbolic limit \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with the metric \( {\widetilde{h}}_{ij} \) and the origin \( \widetilde{P} \) and with finite volume. The new limit \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) has at least as many cusps as the old limit \( \mathcal{H} \) , since we choose \( \mathcal{H} \) with cusps as few as possible. By the definition of convergence, we can find a sequence of compact sets \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) exhausting \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) and containing \( \widetilde{P} \) , and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) of neighborhoods of \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) into \( M \) with \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( \widetilde{P}\right)  = {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) such that for each compact set \( \widetilde{B} \) in \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) and each integer \( m \)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{ * }\left( {g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) \right)  - {\widetilde{h}}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{m}\left( \widetilde{B}\right) } \rightarrow  0
\]

as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . For large enough \( k \) the set \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right) \) will contain all points out to any fixed distance we need from the point \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) \) , and then

\[
{\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right)  \supset  {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right)
\]

since the points of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) have a bounded distance from \( P \) and \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) are reasonably close to preserving the metrics. Hence we can form the composition

\[
{G}_{k} = {\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{-1} \circ  {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right)  : {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \rightarrow  \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}.
\]

Arbitrarily fix \( {\delta }^{\prime } \in  \left( {\delta ,{\delta }_{0}}\right) \) . Since the \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) are as close to preserving the metric as we like, we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{k}^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < {\delta }^{\prime }
\]

for all sufficiently large \( k \) . By Lemma 5.3.7, we deduce that there exists an isometry \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) , and then \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( \omega \right) ,{F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( P\right) }\right) \) (on compact subsets) is very close to \( \left( {\mathcal{H},{h}_{ij}, P}\right) \) as long as \( \delta \) small enough and \( k \) large enough. Since \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) is strictly concave and the foliation of a neighborhood of \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) by constant mean curvature hypersurfaces has the area as a function with nonzero gradient, by the implicit function theorem, there exists a unique constant mean curvature hypersurface with the same area \( a \) near \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) in \( M \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) for \( t \) close to \( \omega \) . Hence, when \( k \) sufficiently large, \( {F}_{k}\left( \omega \right) \) can be extended forward in time a little. This is a contradiction and we have proved claim (5.3.9).

We further claim that there must be some \( k \) such that \( {\omega }_{k} =  + \infty \) (i.e., we can smoothly continue the family of harmonic diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) for all \( {t}_{k} \leq  t <  + \infty \) , in other words, there must be at least one hyperbolic piece persisting). We argue by contradiction. Suppose for each \( k \) large enough, we can continue the family \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  {\omega }_{k} <  + \infty \) with

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{k}^{ * }\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right)  - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta .
\]

Then as before, we consider the new sequence of the manifolds \( M \) with metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \) and origins \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) . For sufficiently large \( k \) , we can obtain diffeomorphisms \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) of neighborhoods of \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) into \( M \) with \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( \widetilde{P}\right)  = {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) which are as close to preserving the metric as we like, where \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k} \) is a sequence of compact sets, exhausting some hyperbolic three-manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) , of finite volume and with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), and containing \( \widetilde{P} \) ; moreover, the set \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right) \) will contain all the points out to any fixed distance we need from the point \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( P\right) \) ; and hence

\[
{\widetilde{F}}_{k}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}\right)  \supseteq  {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right)
\]

since \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) is at bounded distance from \( P \) and \( {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right) \) is reasonably close to preserving the metrics. Then we can form the composition

\[
{G}_{k} = {\widetilde{F}}_{k}^{-1} \circ  {F}_{k}\left( {\omega }_{k}\right)  : \;{\mathcal{H}}_{a} \rightarrow  \widetilde{\mathcal{H}}.
\]

Since the \( {\widetilde{F}}_{k} \) are as close to preserving the metric as we like, for any \( \widetilde{\delta } > \delta \) we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{k}^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } < \widetilde{\delta }
\]

for large enough \( k \) . Then a subsequence of \( {G}_{k} \) converges at least in \( {C}^{q - 1}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) \) topology to a map \( {G}_{\infty } \) of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) . By the same reason as in the argument of previous two paragraphs, the limit map \( {G}_{\infty } \) is a smooth harmonic diffeomorphism from \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) into \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with the metric \( {\widetilde{h}}_{ij} \) , and takes \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to a constant mean curvature hypersurface \( {G}_{\infty }\left( {\partial {\mathcal{H}}_{a}}\right) \) of \( \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{H}},{\widetilde{h}}_{ij}}\right) \) with the area \( a \) , and also satisfies the free boundary condition. Moreover we still have

(5.3.11)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{G}_{\infty }^{ * }{\widetilde{h}}_{ij} - {h}_{ij}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) } = \delta .
\]

Now by Lemma 5.3.7 we deduce that there exists an isometry \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with

\[
{d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {{G}_{\infty }, I}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0}.
\]

By using \( I \) to identify \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}}_{a} \) and \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) , we see that the map \( {I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty } \) is a harmonic diffeomorphism of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{a} \) to itself which satisfies the free boundary condition and

\[
{d}_{{C}^{{l}_{0}}\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{a}\right) }\left( {{I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty },{Id}}\right)  < {\varepsilon }_{0}.
\]

From the uniqueness in Lemma 5.3.8 we conclude that \( {I}^{-1} \circ  {G}_{\infty } = {Id} \) which contradicts with (5.3.11). This shows at least one hyperbolic piece persists. Moreover the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {F}_{k}\left( t\right) \) , for \( {t}_{k} \leq  t <  + \infty \) , is as close to the hyperbolic metric \( {h}_{ij} \) as we like.

We can continue to form other persistent hyperbolic pieces in the same way as long as there are any points \( {P}_{k} \) outside of the chosen pieces where the injectivity radius at times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) are all at least some fixed positive number \( \rho  > 0 \) . The only modification in the proof is to take the new limit \( \mathcal{H} \) to have the least possible number of cusps out of all remaining possible limits.

Note that the volume of the normalized Ricci flow is constant in time. Therefore by combining with Margulis lemma (see for example [55] [76]), we have proved that there exists a finite collection of complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifolds \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) with finite volume, a small number \( a > 0 \) and a time \( T <  + \infty \) such that for all \( t \) beyond \( T \) we can find diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) of \( {\left( {\mathcal{H}}_{l}\right) }_{a} \) into \( M,1 \leq  l \leq  m \) , so that the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) is as close to the hyperbolic metrics as we like and the exceptional part of \( M \) where the points are not in the image of any \( {\varphi }_{l} \) has the injectivity radii everywhere as small as we like.

## Part III: Incompressibility

We remain to show that the boundary tori of any persistent hyperbolic piece are incompressible, in the sense that the fundamental group of the torus injects into that of the whole manifold. The argument of this part is a parabolic version of Schoen and Yau's minimal surface argument in [109, 110, 111].

Let \( B \) be a small positive number and assume the above positive number \( a \) is much smaller than \( B \) . Denote by \( {M}_{a} \) a persistent hyperbolic piece of the manifold \( M \) truncated by boundary tori of area \( a \) with constant mean curvature and denote by \( {M}_{a}^{c} = M \smallsetminus  {\overset{ \circ  }{M}}_{a} \) the part of \( M \) exterior to \( {M}_{a} \) . Thus there is a persistent hyperbolic piece \( {M}_{B} \subset  {M}_{a} \) of the manifold \( M \) truncated by boundary tori of area \( B \) with constant mean curvature. We also denote by \( {M}_{B}^{c} = M \smallsetminus  {M}_{B} \) . By Van Kampen’s Theorem, if \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) then it injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) also. Thus we only need to show \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) .

We will argue by contradiction. Let \( T \) be a torus in \( \partial {M}_{B} \) . Suppose \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) does not inject into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) , then by Dehn’s Lemma the kernel is a cyclic subgroup of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) generated by a primitive element. The work of Meeks-Yau [86] or Meeks-Simon-Yau [87] shows that among all disks in \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) whose boundary curve lies in \( T \) and generates the kernel, there is a smooth embedded disk normal to the boundary which has the least possible area. Let \( A = A\left( t\right) \) be the area of this disk. This is defined for all \( t \) sufficiently large. We will show that \( A\left( t\right) \) decreases at a rate bounded away from zero which will be a contradiction.

Let us compute the rate at which \( A\left( t\right) \) changes under the Ricci flow. We need to show \( A\left( t\right) \) decrease at least at a certain rate, and since \( A\left( t\right) \) is the minimum area to bound any disk in the given homotopy class, it suffices to find some such disk whose area decreases at least that fast. We choose this disk as follows. Pick the minimal disk at time \( {t}_{0} \) , and extend it smoothly a little past the boundary torus since the minimal disk is normal to the boundary. For times \( t \) a little bigger than \( {t}_{0} \) , the boundary torus may need to move a little to stay constant mean curvature with area \( B \) as the metrics change, but we leave the surface alone and take the bounding disk to be the one cut off from it by the new torus. The change of the area \( \widetilde{A}\left( t\right) \) of such disk comes from the change in the metric and the change in the boundary.

For the change in the metric, we choose an orthonormal frame \( X, Y, Z \) at a point \( x \) in the disk so that \( X \) and \( Y \) are tangent to the disk while \( Z \) is normal and compute the rate of change of the area element \( {d\sigma } \) on the disk as

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{d\sigma } = \frac{1}{2}{\left( {g}^{ij}\right) }^{T}\left( {\frac{2}{3}r{\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }^{T} - 2{\left( {R}_{ij}\right) }^{T}}\right) {d\sigma }
\]

\[
= \left\lbrack  {\frac{2}{3}r - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right\rbrack  {d\sigma },
\]

since the metric evolves by the normalized Ricci flow. Here \( {\left( \cdot \right) }^{T} \) denotes the tangential projections on the disk. Notice the torus \( T \) may move in time to preserve constant mean curvature and constant area \( B \) . Suppose the boundary of the disk evolves with a normal velocity \( N \) . The change of the area at boundary along a piece of length \( {ds} \) is given by \( {Nds} \) . Thus the total change of the area \( \widetilde{A}\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
\frac{d\widetilde{A}}{dt} = \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds}.
\]

Note that

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right)  = R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right)  + R\left( {X, Z, X, Z}\right)
\]

\[
+ R\left( {Y, X, Y, X}\right)  + R\left( {Y, Z, Y, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}R + R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right) .
\]

By the Gauss equation, the Gauss curvature \( K \) of the disk is given by

\[
K = R\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right)  + \det {II}
\]

where \( {II} \) is the second fundamental form of the disk in \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) . This gives at \( t = {t}_{0} \) ,

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } - \iint \left( {K - \det {II}}\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds}
\]

Since the bounding disk is a minimal surface, we have

\[
\det {II} \leq  0\text{ . }
\]

The Gauss-Bonnet Theorem tells us that for a disk

\[
\int \int {Kd\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{kds} = {2\pi }
\]

where \( k \) is the geodesic curvature of the boundary. Thus we obtain

(5.3.12)

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } + {\int }_{\partial }{kds} + {\int }_{\partial }{Nds} - {2\pi }.
\]

Recall that we are assuming \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) increases monotonically to -6 as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . By the evolution equation of the scalar curvature,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq  4\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

and then

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\left( {r\left( t\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right) {dt} <  + \infty .
\]

This implies that \( r\left( t\right)  \rightarrow   - 6 \) as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) by using the derivatives estimate for the curvatures. Thus for every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) we have

\[
\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R \leq   - \left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right)
\]

for \( t \) sufficiently large. And then the first term on RHS of (5.3.12) is bounded above by

\[
\iint \left( {\frac{2}{3}r - \frac{1}{2}R}\right) {d\sigma } \leq   - \left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) A.
\]

The geodesic curvature \( k \) of the boundary of the minimal disk is the acceleration of a curve moving with unit speed along the intersection of the disk with the torus; since the disk and torus are normal, this is the same as the second fundamental form of the torus in the direction of the curve of intersection. Now if the metric were actually hyperbolic, the second fundamental form of the torus would be exactly 1 in all directions. Note that the persistent hyperbolic pieces are as close to the standard hyperbolic as we like. This makes that the second term of RHS of (5.3.12) is bounded above by

\[
{\int }_{\partial }{kds} \leq  \left( {1 + {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L
\]

for some sufficiently small positive number \( {\varepsilon }_{0} > 0 \) , where \( L \) is the length of the boundary curve. Also since the metric on the persistent hyperbolic pieces are close to the standard hyperbolic as we like, its change under the normalized Ricci flow is as small as we like; So the motion of the constant mean curvature torus of fixed area \( B \) will have a normal velocity \( N \) as small as we like. This again makes the third term of RHS of (5.3.12) bounded above by

\[
{\int }_{\partial }{Nds} \leq  {\varepsilon }_{0}L
\]

Combining these estimates, we obtain

(5.3.13)

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }
\]

on the persistent hyperbolic piece, where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is some sufficiently small positive number.

We next need to bound the length \( L \) in terms of the area \( A \) . Since \( a \) is much smaller than \( B \) , for large \( t \) the metric is as close as we like to the standard hyperbolic one; not just on the persistent hyperbolic piece \( {M}_{B} \) but as far beyond as we like. Thus for a long distance into \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) the metric will look nearly like a standard hyperbolic cusplike collar.

Let us first recall a special coordinate system on the standard hyperbolic cusp projecting beyond torus \( {T}_{1} \) in \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{1} \) as follows. The universal cover of the flat torus \( {T}_{1} \) can be mapped conformally to the \( x - y \) plane so that the deck transformation of \( {T}_{1} \) become translations in \( x \) and \( y \) , and so that the Euclidean area of the quotient is 1 ; then these coordinates are unique up to a translation. The hyperbolic cusp projecting beyond the torus \( {T}_{1} \) in \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{1} \) can be parametrized by \( \left\{  {\left( {x, y, z}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \mid  z > 0}\right\} \) with the hyperbolic metric

(5.3.14)

\[
d{s}^{2} = \frac{d{x}^{2} + d{y}^{2} + d{z}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}.
\]

Note that we can make the solution metric, in an arbitrarily large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ), as close to hyperbolic as we wish (in the sense that there exists a diffeomorphism from a large neighborhood of the torus \( {T}_{B} \) (of \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{B} \) ) on the standard hyperbolic cusp to the above neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) such that the pull-back of the solution metric by the diffeomorphism is as close to the hyperbolic metric as we wish). Then by using this diffeomorphism (up to a slight modification) we can parametrize the cusplike tube of \( {M}_{B}^{c} \) projecting beyond the torus \( T \) in \( \partial {M}_{B} \) by \( \{ \left( {x, y, z}\right)  \mid  z \geq  \zeta \} \) where the height \( \zeta \) is chosen so that the torus in the hyperbolic cusp at height \( \zeta \) has the area \( B \) .

Now consider our minimal disk, and let \( L\left( z\right) \) be the length of the curve of the intersection of the disk with the torus at height \( z \) in the above coordinate system, and also let \( A\left( z\right) \) be the area of the part of the disk between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) . We now want to derive a monotonicity formula on the area \( A\left( z\right) \) for the minimal surface.

For almost every \( z \) the intersection of the disk with the torus at height \( z \) is a smooth embedded curve or a finite union of them by the standard transversality theorem. If there is more than one curve, at least one of them is not homotopic to a point in \( T \) and represents the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) such that a part of the original disk beyond height \( z \) continues to a disk that bounds it. We extend this disk back to the initial height \( \zeta \) by dropping the curve straight down. Let \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) be the length of the curve we picked at height \( z \) ; of course \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)  \leq  L\left( z\right) \) with equality if it is the only piece. Let \( \widetilde{L}\left( w\right) \) denote the length of the same curve in the \( x - y \) plane dropped down to height \( w \) for \( \zeta  \leq  w \leq  z \) . In the hyperbolic space we would have

\[
\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  = \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right)
\]

exactly. In our case there is a small error proportional to \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) and we can also take it proportional to the distance \( z - w \) by which it drops since \( {\left. \widetilde{L}\left( w\right) \right| }_{w = z} = \widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \) and the solution metric is close to the hyperbolic in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. Thus, for arbitrarily given \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( {\zeta }^{ * } > \zeta \) , as the solution metric is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

\[
\left| {\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  - \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) }\right|  \leq  \delta \left( {z - w}\right) \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)
\]

for all \( z \) and \( w \) in \( \zeta  \leq  w \leq  z \leq  {\zeta }^{ * } \) . Now given \( \varepsilon \) and \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) pick \( \delta  = {2\varepsilon }/{\zeta }^{ * } \) . Then

(5.3.15)

\[
\widetilde{L}\left( w\right)  \leq  \frac{z}{w}\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) \left\lbrack  {1 + \frac{{2\varepsilon }\left( {z - w}\right) }{w}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

When we drop the curve vertically for the construction of the new disk we get an area \( \widetilde{A}\left( z\right) \) between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) given by

\[
\widetilde{A}\left( z\right)  = \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{\widetilde{L}\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}.
\]

Here and in the following \( o\left( 1\right) \) denotes various small error quantities as the solution metric close to hyperbolic. On the other hand if we do not drop vertically we pick up even more area, so the area \( A\left( z\right) \) of the original disk between \( \zeta \) and \( z \) has

(5.3.16)

\[
A\left( z\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}.
\]

Since the original disk minimized among all disks bounded a curve in the primitive generator of the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) , and the new disk beyond the height \( z \) is part of the original disk, we have

\[
A\left( z\right)  \leq  \widetilde{A}\left( z\right)
\]

and then by combining with (5.3.15),

\[
{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw} \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) z\widetilde{L}\left( z\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{{w}^{2}} + \frac{2\varepsilon z}{{w}^{3}}}\right\rbrack  {dw}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) L\left( z\right) \frac{\left( z - \zeta \right) }{\zeta }\left\lbrack  {1 + \varepsilon \left( \frac{z - \zeta }{\zeta }\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

Here we used the fact that \( \widetilde{L}\left( z\right)  \leq  L\left( z\right) \) . Since the solution metric is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

\[
\frac{d}{dz}\left( {{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}}\right)  = \frac{L\left( z\right) }{z}
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) \frac{\zeta }{z\left( {z - \zeta }\right) }\left\lbrack  {1 - \varepsilon \left( \frac{z - \zeta }{\zeta }\right) }\right\rbrack  {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

\[
\geq  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{z - \zeta } - \frac{1 + {2\varepsilon }}{z}}\right\rbrack  {\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

or equivalently

(5.3.17)

\[
\frac{d}{dz}\log \left\{  {\frac{{z}^{1 + {2\varepsilon }}}{\left( z - \zeta \right) }{\int }_{\zeta }^{z}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}}\right\}   \geq  0.
\]

This is the desired monotonicity formula for the area \( A\left( z\right) \) .

It follows directly from (5.3.16) and (5.3.17) that

\[
\frac{{z}^{1 + {2\varepsilon }}}{\left( z - \zeta \right) }A\left( z\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\zeta }^{2\varepsilon }L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

or equivalently

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\left( \frac{z}{\zeta }\right) }^{2\varepsilon }\frac{z}{z - \zeta }A\left( z\right)
\]

for all \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\zeta ,{\zeta }^{ * }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the solution metric, in an arbitrarily large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ), as close to hyperbolic as we wish, we may assume that \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) is so large that \( \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }} > \zeta \) and \( \frac{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }} - \zeta } \) is close to 1, and also \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) is so small that \( {\left( \frac{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}{\zeta }\right) }^{2\varepsilon } \) is close to 1 . Thus for arbitrarily small \( {\delta }_{0} > 0 \) , we have

(5.3.18)

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) A\left( \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) .
\]

Now recall that (5.3.13) states

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }.
\]

We now claim that if

\[
\left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A \geq  0
\]

then \( L = L\left( \zeta \right) \) is uniformly bounded from above.

Indeed by the assumption we have

\[
A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)  \leq  \frac{\left( 1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}\right) }{\left( 1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}\right) }L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

since \( A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)  \leq  A \) . By combining with (5.3.16) we have some \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) satisfying

\[
\frac{L\left( {z}_{0}\right) }{{z}_{0}}\left( {{\zeta }^{ * } - \sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}\right)  \leq  {\int }_{\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }}}^{{\zeta }^{ * }}\frac{L\left( w\right) }{w}{dw}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) A\left( {\zeta }^{ * }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) \left( \frac{1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}{1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L\left( \zeta \right) .
\]

Thus for \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) suitably large, by noting that the solution metric on a large neighborhood of \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) is sufficiently close to hyperbolic, we have

(5.3.19)

\[
L\left( {z}_{0}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + 4{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{{z}_{0}}{{\zeta }^{ * }}L\left( \zeta \right)
\]

for some \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) . It is clear that we may assume the intersection curve between the minimal disk with the torus at this height \( {z}_{0} \) is smooth and embedded. If the intersection curve at the height \( {z}_{0} \) has more than one piece, as before one of them will represent the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) , and we can ignore the others. Let us move (the piece of) the intersection curve on the torus at height \( {z}_{0} \) through as small as possible area in the same homotopy class of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) to a curve which is a geodesic circle in the flat torus coming from our special coordinates, and then drop this geodesic circle vertically in the special coordinates to obtain another new disk. We will compare the area of this new disk with the original minimal disk as follows.

Denote by \( G \) the length of the geodesic circle in the standard hyperbolic cusp at height 1 . Then the length of the geodesic circle at height \( {z}_{0} \) will be \( G/{z}_{0} \) . Observe that given an embedded curve of length \( l \) circling the cylinder \( {S}^{1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) of circumference \( w \) once, it is possible to deform the curve through an area not bigger than \( {lw} \) into a meridian circle. Note that (the piece of) the intersection curve represents the primitive generator in the kernel of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) . Note also that the solution metric is sufficiently close to the hyperbolic metric. Then the area of the deformation from (the piece of) the intersection curve on the torus at height \( {z}_{0} \) to the geodesic circle at height \( {z}_{0} \) is bounded by

\[
\left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) \left( \frac{G}{{z}_{0}}\right)  \cdot  L\left( {z}_{0}\right) .
\]

The area to drop the geodesic circle from height \( {z}_{0} \) to height \( \zeta \) is bounded by

\[
\left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) {\int }_{\zeta }^{{z}_{0}}\frac{G}{{w}^{2}}{dw}.
\]

Hence comparing the area of the original minimal disk to that of this new disk gives

\[
A\left( {z}_{0}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + o\left( 1\right) }\right) G\left\lbrack  {\frac{L\left( {z}_{0}\right) }{{z}_{0}} + \left( {\frac{1}{\zeta } - \frac{1}{{z}_{0}}}\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

By (5.3.18),(5.3.19) and the fact that \( {z}_{0} \in  \left( {\sqrt{{\zeta }^{ * }},{\zeta }^{ * }}\right) \) , this in turn gives

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) A\left( {z}_{0}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{0}}\right) G\left\lbrack  {\left( {1 + 4{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{L\left( \zeta \right) }{{\zeta }^{ * }} + \frac{1}{\zeta }}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Since \( {\zeta }^{ * } \) is suitably large, we obtain

\[
L\left( \zeta \right)  \leq  {2G}/\zeta
\]

This gives the desired assertion since \( G \) is fixed from the geometry of the limit hyperbolic manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) and \( \zeta \) is very large as long as the area \( B \) of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) small enough.

Thus the combination of (5.3.13), (5.3.18) and the assertion implies that either

\[
\frac{d}{dt}A \leq   - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\frac{d}{dt}A \leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) L - \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) A - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {1 + 2{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \frac{2G}{\zeta } - {2\pi }
\]

\[
\leq   - \pi
\]

since the solution metric on a very large neighborhood of the torus \( T \) (of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) ) is sufficiently close to hyperbolic and \( \zeta \) is very large as the area \( B \) of \( \partial {M}_{B} \) small enough. This is impossible because \( A \geq  0 \) and the persistent hyperbolic pieces go on forever. The contradiction shows that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( T\right) \) in fact injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M}_{B}^{c}\right) \) . This proves that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {M}_{B}}\right) \) injects into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of Theorem 5.3.4. [

\[
+ {\widehat{m}}_{\ell }{t}^{{\widehat{m}}_{\ell } - 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + C

Hence if \( \widetilde{C} \) is chosen so that \( 4{t}^{{\widehat{m}}_{\ell }}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \leq  \widetilde{C} \) , then by (14.33) and (14.34) we have (note that \( {t}^{{m}_{\ell } - {\widehat{m}}_{\ell }} \leq  C \) for \( t \leq  \tau \) )

\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) \left( {\left( {\widetilde{C} + {t}^{{\widehat{m}}_{\ell }}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}}\right) {t}^{{m}_{\ell }}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}}\right)

\]

\[
\leq   - {10}{t}^{{\widehat{m}}_{\ell } + {m}_{\ell }}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 2}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}

(again using \( {t}^{{m}_{\ell }} \leq  C{t}^{{\widehat{m}}_{\ell }} \) for \( t \leq  \tau \) ). Since \( \operatorname{sign}\left( {m}_{\ell }\right)  = {m}_{\ell } - {\widehat{m}}_{\ell } \) , we conclude

\leq   - \frac{c}{{t}^{\operatorname{sign}\left( {m}_{\ell }\right) }}{F}_{m,\ell }^{2} + \frac{C}{{t}^{\operatorname{sign}\left( {m}_{\ell }\right) }},

using \( {t}^{{\widehat{m}}_{\ell } + {m}_{\ell }} = {t}^{2{m}_{\ell }} \cdot  {t}^{-\operatorname{sign}\left( {m}_{\ell }\right) } \) . The lemma follows.

\[

\[

\]

(14.26)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{t}^{k}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}}\right)  \leq  \Delta \left( {{t}^{k}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2{t}^{k}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}

- 2{t}^{{2m} + 1}\nabla {\left| {\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2} \cdot  \nabla {\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq   - {10}{t}^{{2m} + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 2}\operatorname{Rm}\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ 8{t}^{{2m} + 1}\left| {{\nabla }^{m}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right| {\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}\left| {{\nabla }^{m + 2}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|
\]

\[
- 2{t}^{{2m} + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{4} + \left( {C + {t}^{m}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}}\right) \left( {C{t}^{m}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + {Ct}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {m{t}^{m - 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + C}\right) \left( {{t}^{m + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

\leq   - \frac{2}{5t}{\left( {t}^{m + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}\right) }^{2} + C\left( {1 + t}\right) {t}^{m}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + {Ct} + \frac{C}{t}

\leq   - \frac{c}{t}{\left\lbrack  \left( C + {t}^{m}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}\mathrm{\;R}\mathrm{\;m}\right| }^{2}\right) {t}^{m + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{m + 1}\mathrm{\;R}\mathrm{\;m}\right| }^{2}\right\rbrack  }^{2} + \frac{C}{t},

\[

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. Theorem I.12.1) Given \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) and a function \( \Phi \) as above, one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. Let \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) be a Ricci flow solution on a three-manifold \( M \) , defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) with \( T \geq  1 \) . We suppose that for each \( t, g\left( t\right) \) is complete, and the sectional curvature is bounded on compact time intervals. Suppose that the Ricci flow has \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \sigma \) . Then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1},{t}_{0} - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q \) , \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We give a proof which differs in some points from the proof in [51] but which has the same ingredients. We first outline the argument.

Suppose that the theorem is false. Then for some \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) , we have a sequence of such \( \Phi \) -nonnegatively curved 3-dimensional Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined on intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) , and sequences \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0,{\widehat{x}}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k} \geq  1 \) such that \( {M}_{k} \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( < \sigma \) and \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) , but the \( {Q}_{k} \) -rescaled solution in \( {B}_{{\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1/2}}\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{\widehat{t}}_{k} - {\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is not \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any \( \kappa \) -solution.

We note that if the statement were false for \( \epsilon \) then it would also be false for any smaller \( \epsilon \) . Because of this, somewhat paradoxically, we will begin the argument with a given \( \epsilon \) but will allow ourselves to make \( \epsilon \) small enough later so that the argument works. To be clear, we will eventually get a contradiction using a fixed (small) value of \( \epsilon \) , but as the proof goes along we will impose some upper bounds on this value in order for the proof to work. (If we tried to list all of the constraints at the beginning of the argument then they would look unmotivated.)

The goal is to get a contradiction based on the "bad" points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . In a sense, the method of proof of Theorem 52.7 is an induction on the curvature scale. For example, if we were to make the additional assumption in the theorem that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) and \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) then the theorem would be very easy to prove. We would just take a convergent subsequence of the rescaled solutions, based at \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) , to get a \( \kappa \) -solution; this would give a contradiction. This simple argument can be considered to be the first step in a proof by induction on curvature scale. In the proof of Theorem 52.7 one effectively proves the result at a given curvature scale inductively by assuming that the result is true at higher curvature scales.

The actual proof consists of four steps. Step 1 consists of replacing the sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) by another sequence of "bad" points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) which have the property that points near \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with distinctly higher scalar curvature are "good" points. It then suffices to get a contradiction based on the existence of the sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

In steps 2-4 one uses the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to build up a \( \kappa \) -solution, whose existence then contradicts the "badness" of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . More precisely, let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We will show that the sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) accumulates on a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , thereby obtaining a contradiction.

In step 2 one takes a pointed limit of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) in order to construct what will become the final time slice of the \( \kappa \) -solution, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . In order to take this limit, it is necessary to show that the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) have uniformly bounded curvature on distance balls of a fixed radius. If this were not true then for some radius, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) would have curvatures that asymptotically blowup on the ball of that radius. One shows that geometrically, the curvature blowup is due to the asymptotic formation of a cone-like point at the blowup radius. Doing a further rescaling at this cone-like point, one obtains a Ricci flow solution that ends on a part of a nonflat metric cone. This gives a contradiction as in the case \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) of Theorem 41.2.

Thus one can construct the pointed limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . The goal now is to show that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is the final time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) . In step 3 one shows that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) extends backward to a Ricci flow solution on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and that the time slices have bounded nonnegative curvature. In step 4 one shows that the Ricci flow solution can be extended all the way to time \( \left( {-\infty ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , thereby constructing a \( \kappa \) -solution

Step 1: Adjusting the choice of basepoints.

We first modify the points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) slightly in time to points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) so that in the given Ricci flow solution, there are no other "bad" points with much larger scalar curvature in a earlier time interval whose length is large compared to \( R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1} \) . (The phrase "nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) " in [51, Proof of Theorem 12.1] should read "nearly the largest curvature \( Q \) ". This is clear from the sentence in parentheses that follows.) The proof of the next lemma is by pointpicking, as in Appendix H.

Lemma 52.9. We can find \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty ,{x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , and \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) such that \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and for all \( k \) the conclusion of Theorem 52.7 fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in \; {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for which \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

Proof. Choose \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( {H}_{k}{\left( R\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10} \) for all \( k \) . For each \( k \) , initially set \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . Put \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and look for a point in \( {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) at which Theorem 52.7 fails, and the scalar curvature is at least \( {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . If such a point exists, replace \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) by this point; otherwise do nothing. Repeat this until the second alternative occurs. This process must terminate with a new choice of \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfying the lemma.

Hereafter we use this modified sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We use \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) to denote its scalar curvature; in particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) . Note that the rescaled time interval of Lemma 52.9 has duration \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; this is what we want in order to try to extract an ancient solution.

Step 2: For every \( \rho  < \infty \) , the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded on the \( \rho \) -balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) (the argument for this is essentially equivalent to [51, Pf. of Claim 2 of Theorem I.12.1]). Before proceeding, we need some bounds which come from our choice of basepoints, and the derivative bounds inherited (by approximation) from \( \kappa \) -solutions.

Lemma 52.10. There is a constant \( C = C\left( \kappa \right) \) so that for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in a Ricci flow solution, if \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) and the solution in \( {B}_{t}\left( {x,{\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to a corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution then \( \left| {\nabla {R}^{-1/2}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) and \( \left| {{\partial }_{t}{R}^{-1}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) .

Proof. This follows from the compactness in Theorem 46.1.

Note that the same value of \( C \) in Lemma 52.10 also works for smaller \( \epsilon \) .

Lemma 52.11. (cf. Claim 1 of I.12.1) For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + \left| {{R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) then there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a spacetime curve \( \gamma \) that goes linearly from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) , and then goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic. If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( p \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( p = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . From the conclusion of Lemma 52.9, we can apply Lemma 52.10 along \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( p \) . The claim follows from integrating the ensuing derivative bounds along \( \gamma \) .

Lemma 52.12. In terms of the rescaled solution \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) , for each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{k} = 1 + \left| {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| . \)

Proof. This is just the rescaled version of Lemma 52.11.

For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , put

(52.13)

\[
D\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

and let \( {\rho }_{0} \) be the supremum of the \( \rho \) ’s for which \( D\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) . Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) , in view of Lemma 52.12 (taking \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) ). Suppose that \( {\rho }_{0} < \infty \) . After passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can find a sequence \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) and \( \bar{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Let \( {\eta }_{k} \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\eta }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\eta }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) at which \( \bar{R}\left( {{z}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\eta }_{k} \) running from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {z}_{k} \) . By Lemma 52.12 the length of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . Due to the \( \Phi \) -pinching (see (52.4)), for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) on the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . The injectivity radius is also controlled in \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right) \) , in view of the curvature bounds and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing. Therefore after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the pointed sequence \( \left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology (i.e. for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) we have the usual Gromov-Hausdorff convergence) to a pointed \( {C}^{1} \) -Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\eta }_{k} \) converge to a segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\eta }_{\infty } \subset  Z \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converges to \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Let \( \bar{Z} \) denote the completion of \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  \bar{Z} \) the limit point of \( {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Note that by Lemma 52.9 and part 4 of Corollary 42.1, the Riemannian structure near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) may be chosen to be many times differentiable. (Alternatively, this follows from Lemma 52.12 and the Shi estimates of Appendix D.) In particular the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty } \) is defined, differentiable, and satisfies the bound in Lemma 52.10 near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Lemma 52.14. 1. There is a function \( c : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}c\left( t\right)  = \; \infty \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) then \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) d{\left( {y}_{\infty }, w\right) }^{2} > c\left( \epsilon \right) \) .

2. There is a function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \cup  \{ \infty \} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) and \( d\left( {{y}_{\infty }, w}\right) \) is sufficiently small then the pointed manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( 2{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder in the \( {C}^{2} \) topology.

Proof. It follows from Lemma 52.9 that for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , the pointed Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to (a time slice of) a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. From the definition of pointed closeness, there is an embedded region around \( w \) , large on the scale defined by \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) , which is close to the corresponding subset of a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. This gives a lower bound on the distance \( {\rho }_{0} - d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) to the point of curvature blowup, thereby proving part 1 of the lemma.

We know that \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N,\star , h\left( t\right) }\right) \) in the pointed \( {C}^{2} \) -topology. By Lemma 52.10, we know \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) , for \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . In particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . From part 1 above, we can choose \( \epsilon \) small enough in order to make \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) large enough to apply Proposition 49.1. Hence the pointed manifold \( \left( {N,\star , R\left( \star \right) h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder, where \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The lemma follows.

Note that the function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) in Lemma 52.14 is independent of the particular manifold \( Z \) that arises in our proof.

From part 2 of Lemma 52.14, if \( \epsilon \) is small and \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) then \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {C}^{2} \) -close to a round cylinder. The cross-section of the cylinder has diameter approximately \( \pi {\left( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . If we form the union of the balls \( B\left( {w,{2\pi }{\left( {R}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , as \( w \) ranges over such points in \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , then we obtain a connected Riemannian manifold \( W \) . By adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we get a metric space \( \bar{W} \) which is locally complete, and geodesic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . As the original manifolds \( {M}_{k} \) had \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, it follows from Lemma 52.5 that \( W \) is nonnegatively curved. Furthermore, \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{W} \) , since such a geodesic would have to pass through a cylindrical region near \( {y}_{\infty } \) twice. The usual proof of the Toponogov triangle comparison inequality now applies near \( {y}_{\infty } \) since minimizers remain in the smooth nonnegatively curved part of \( \bar{W} \) . Then \( \bar{W} \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense.

This implies that blowups of \( \left( {\bar{W},{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converge to the tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) . As \( \bar{W} \) is three-dimensional, so is \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) [12, Corollary 7.11]. It will be \( {C}^{2} \) -smooth away from the vertex and nowhere flat, by part 2 of Lemma 52.14. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) such that \( d\left( {z,{y}_{\infty }}\right)  = 1 \) . Then for any \( \delta  < \frac{1}{2} \) , the ball \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of rescaled balls \( B\left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{\widehat{r}}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\widehat{r}}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , whose center points \( \left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 52.7. Applying Lemma 52.12 and Appendix B, if \( \delta  = \delta \left( \kappa \right) \) is taken small enough then we get the curvature bounds needed to extract a limiting Ricci flow solution whose time zero slice is isometric to \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right) \) . Now we can apply the reasoning from the \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) case of Theorem 41.2 to get a contradiction. This completes step 2.

Step 3: The sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right) \) accumulates on a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) which is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) . By step 2, we know that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) at \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) is bounded by a function of the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Lemma 52.12 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on \( d\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right) \) . Thus we can conclude, using \( \Phi \) -pinching (52.4) and Shi’s estimates (Appendix D), that all derivatives of the curvature \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) are controlled as a function of the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) , which means that the sequence of pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) accumulates to a smooth manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) .

From Lemma 52.5, \( {M}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative sectional curvature. We claim that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has bounded curvature. If not then there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right)  = \; \infty \) and \( \bar{R}\left( q\right)  \leq  2\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right) \) for \( q \in  B\left( {{y}_{k},{A}_{k}\bar{R}{\left( {q}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , where \( {A}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; compare [33, Lemma 22.2]. Lemma 52.9 implies that for large \( k \) , a rescaled neighborhood of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{q}_{k}}\right) \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution. As in the proof of Theorem 46.1, we obtain a sequence of neck-like regions in \( {M}_{\infty } \) with smaller and smaller cross-sections, which contradicts the existence of the Sharafutdinov retraction.

By Lemma 52.12 again, we now get curvature control on \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) for a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \Delta ,{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \Delta  > 0 \) , and hence we can extract a subsequence which converges to a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , which has nonnegative curvature and bounded curvature on compact time intervals.

Step 4: Getting an ancient solution. Let \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval on which we can extract a limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) with bounded curvature on compact time intervals. Suppose that \( {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By Lemma 52.12 the maximum of the scalar curvature on the time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) must tend to infinity as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) . From the trace Harnack inequality, \( {R}_{t} + \frac{R}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \geq  0 \) , and so

(52.15)

\[
{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }},
\]

where \( Q \) is the maximum of the scalar curvature on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Combining this with Corollary 27.16, we get

(52.16)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }\sqrt{Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Since the right hand side is integrable on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and using the fact that distances are nonincreasing in time (since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) ), it follows that there is a constant \( C \) such that

(52.17)

\[
\left| {{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right|  < C
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty }, t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact then by (52.17) the diameter of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the minimum of the scalar curvature is increasing in time, it is also bounded independent of \( t \) . Now the argument in Step 2 shows that the curvature is bounded everywhere independent of \( t \) . (We can apply the argument of Step 2 to the time- \( t \) slice because the main ingredient was Lemma 52.9, which holds for rescaled time \( t \) .)

We may therefore assume \( {M}_{\infty } \) is noncompact. To be consistent with the notation of I.12.1, we now relabel the basepoint \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) \) as \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since nonnegatively curved manifolds are asymptotically conical (see Appendix G), there is a constant \( D \) such that if \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) , and \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right)  > D \) , then there is a point \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

(52.18)

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) \;\text{ and }\;{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{2}{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) ;
\]

by (52.17) the same conditions hold at all times \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , up to error \( C \) . If for some such \( y \) , and some \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the scalar curvature were large, then \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {y, t}\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) would be \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N, h\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {z,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) . When \( \epsilon \) is small we could use Proposition 49.1 to see that \( y \) lies in a neck region \( U \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of diameter \( \approx  R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ll  1 \) .

We claim that \( U \) separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) in the sense that \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) belong to disjoint components of \( {M}_{\infty } - U \) , where \( {x}_{0}, y \) , and \( x \) satisfy (52.18). To see this, we recall that if \( {M}_{\infty } \) has more than one end then it splits isometrically, in which case the claim is clear. If \( {M}_{\infty } \) has one end then we consider an exhaustion of \( {M}_{\infty } \) by totally convex compact sets \( {C}_{t} \) as in Section 46. One of the sets \( {C}_{t} \) will have boundary consisting of an approximate 2-sphere cross-section in the neck region \( U \) , giving the separation.

(For another argument, suppose that \( U \) does not separate \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\widetilde{Z}}_{y}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) (from Proposition 49.1), the segments \( \overline{y{x}_{0}} \) and \( \overline{yx} \) must exit \( U \) by different ends. If \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) can be joined by a curve avoiding \( U \) then there is a nonzero element of \( {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{M}_{\infty },\mathbb{Z}}\right) \) . The corresponding infinite cyclic cover of \( {M}_{\infty } \) will then isometrically split off a line and its quotient \( {M}_{\infty } \) will be compact, which is a contradiction. We thank one of the referees for this argument.)

Obviously, at time \( {t}_{0} \) the set \( U \) still separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\bar{g}}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature, we have \( {\operatorname{diam}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( U\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{diam}}_{t}\left( U\right)  \ll  1 \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) has bounded geometry, there cannot be topologically separating subsets of arbitrarily small diameter. Thus there must be a uniform upper bound on \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) and the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is uniformly bounded (in space and time) outside a set of uniformly bounded diameter. Repeating the reasoning from Step 2, we get uniform bounds everywhere. This contradicts our assumption that the curvature blows up as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) .

It remains to show that the ancient solution is a \( \kappa \) -solution. The only remaining point is to show that it is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at all scales. This follows from the fact that the original Ricci flow solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) were \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than the fixed number \( \sigma \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left-Invariant and Bi-Invariant Metrics on Lie Groups
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Lie groups. A Lie group is a group \( G \) with a differentiable structure such that the mapping \( G \times  G \rightarrow  G \) given by \( \left( {x, y}\right)  \rightarrow  x{y}^{-1}, x, y \in  G \) , is differentiable. It follows then that translations from the left \( {L}_{x} \) and translations from the right \( {R}_{x} \) given by: \( {L}_{x} : G \rightarrow  G,{L}_{x}\left( y\right)  = {xy};{R}_{x} : G \rightarrow  G,{R}_{x}\left( y\right)  = {yx} \) are diffeomor-phisms.

We say that a Riemannian metric on \( G \) is left invariant if \( \langle u, v{\rangle }_{y} = \langle d{\left( {L}_{x}\right) }_{y}u, d{\left( {L}_{x}\right) }_{y}v{\rangle }_{{L}_{x}\left( y\right) } \) for all \( x, y \in  G, u, v \in  {T}_{y}G \) , that is, if \( {L}_{x} \) is an isometry. Analogously, we can define a right invariant Riemannian metric. A Riemannian metric on \( G \) which is both right and left invariant is said to be bi-invariant.

We say that a differentiable vector field \( X \) on a Lie group \( G \) is left invariant if \( d{L}_{x}X = X \) for all \( x \in  G \) . The left invariant vector fields are completely determined by their values at a single point of \( G \) . This allows us to introduce an additional structure on the tangent space to the neutral element \( e \in  G \) in the following manner. To each vector \( {X}_{e} \in  {T}_{e}G \) we associate the left invariant \( X \) defined by \( {X}_{a} = d{L}_{a}{X}_{e}, a \in  G \) . Let \( X, Y \) be left invariant vector fields on \( G \) . Since for each \( x \in  G \) and for any differentiable function \( f \) on \( G \) ,

\[
d{L}_{x}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  f = \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \left( {f \circ  {L}_{x}}\right)  = X\left( {d{L}_{x}Y}\right) f - Y\left( {d{L}_{x}X}\right) f =
\]

\[
= \left( {{XY} - {YX}}\right) f = \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  f
\]

we conclude that the bracket of any two left invariant vector fields is again a left invariant vector field. If \( {X}_{e},{Y}_{e} \in  {T}_{e}G \) , we put \( \left\lbrack  {{X}_{e},{Y}_{e}}\right\rbrack   = \; {\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }_{e} \) . With this operation, \( {T}_{e}G \) is called the Lie algebra of \( G \) , denoted by \( \mathcal{G} \) . From now on, the elements in the Lie algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) will be thought of either as vectors in \( {T}_{e}G \) or as left invariant vector fields on \( G \) .

To introduce a left invariant metric on \( G \) , take any arbitrary inner product \( \langle \) , \( {\rangle }_{e} \) on \( \mathcal{G} \) and define

(2)

\[
\langle u, v{\rangle }_{x} = \left\langle  {{\left( d{L}_{{x}^{-1}}\right) }_{x}\left( u\right) ,{\left( d{L}_{{x}^{-1}}\right) }_{x}\left( v\right) {\rangle }_{e},\;x \in  G, u, v \in  {T}_{x}G.}\right.
\]

Since \( {L}_{x} \) depends differentiably on \( x \) , this construction actually produces a Riemannian metric, which is clearly left invariant.

In an analogous manner we can construct a right invariant metric on \( G \) . If \( G \) is compact, we will see in Exercise 7 that \( G \) possesses a bi-invariant metric.

If \( G \) has a bi-invariant metric, the inner product that the metric determines on \( \mathcal{G} \) satisfies the following relation: For any \( U, V, X \in  \mathcal{G} \) ,

(3)

\[
\langle \left\lbrack  {U, X}\right\rbrack  , V\rangle  =  - \langle U,\left\lbrack  {V, X}\right\rbrack  \rangle .
\]

Before proving the relation above, we need some preliminary facts about Lie groups.

For any \( a \in  G \) , let \( {R}_{{a}^{-1}}{L}_{a} : G \rightarrow  G \) be the inner automorphism of \( G \) determined by \( a \) . Such a mapping is a diffeomorphism that keeps \( e \) fixed. Thus, the differential \( d\left( {{R}_{{a}^{-1}}{L}_{a}}\right)  = {Ad}\left( a\right)  : \mathcal{G} \rightarrow  \mathcal{G} \) is a linear map (in fact, it is a homomorphism of the Lie algebra, but we do not need this fact). Explicitly,

\[
{Ad}\left( a\right) Y = d{R}_{{a}^{-1}}d{L}_{a}Y = d{R}_{{a}^{-1}}Y,\;\text{ for all }Y \in  \mathcal{G}.
\]

Let \( {x}_{t} \) be the flow of \( X \in  \mathcal{G} \) . Then, from Proposition 5.4 of Chapter 0,

\[
\left\lbrack  {Y, X}\right\rbrack   = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{1}{t}\left( {d{x}_{t}\left( Y\right)  - Y}\right)
\]

On the other hand, since \( X \) is left invariant, \( {L}_{y} \circ  {x}_{t} = {x}_{t} \circ  {L}_{y} \) , giving

\[
{x}_{t}\left( y\right)  = {x}_{t}\left( {{L}_{y}\left( e\right) }\right)  = {L}_{y}\left( {{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }\right)  = y{x}_{t}\left( e\right)  = {R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }\left( y\right) .
\]

Therefore, \( d{x}_{t} = d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) } \) , and

\[
\left\lbrack  {Y, X}\right\rbrack   = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{1}{t}\left( {d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }\left( Y\right)  - Y}\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{1}{t}\left( {{Ad}\left( {{x}_{t}^{-1}\left( e\right) }\right) Y - Y}\right) .
\]

Let us now return to the proof of (3). Let \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {beabi} - {invariant} \) metric on a Lie group \( G \) . Then for any \( X, U, V \in  \mathcal{G} \) ,

\[
\langle U, V\rangle  = \left\langle  {d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) } \circ  d{L}_{{x}_{t}^{-1}\left( e\right) }U, d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) } \circ  d{L}_{{x}_{t}^{-1}\left( e\right) }V}\right\rangle   =
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }U, d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }V}\right\rangle  .
\]

Differentiating the expression above with respect to \( t \) , recalling that \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {isbilinear},{andsetting}t = 0 \) in the expression obtained, we conclude that

\[
0 = \langle \left\lbrack  {U, X}\right\rbrack  , V\rangle  + \langle U,\left\lbrack  {V, X}\right\rbrack  \rangle ,
\]

which is the equation (3).

The important point about the relation above is that it characterizes the bi-invariant metrics of \( G \) , in the following sense. If a positive bilinear form \( \langle \) , \( {\rangle }_{e} \) defined on \( \mathcal{G} \) satisfies the relation (3), then the Riemannian metric defined on \( G \) by (2) is bi-invariant. It is not difficult to prove this fact but we will not go into the proof here.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Existence of a generalized pinching set). Let

\[
{C}_{\clubsuit }{\left( s\right) }_{s \in  \lbrack 0,1)} \subset  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right)
\]

be a continuous family of closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant cones of maximum dimension, such that \( {C}_{4}\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) is contained in the half-space of curvature operators with positive scalar curvature for all \( s \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) . Suppose that for \( \mathbf{R} \in  \partial {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) the vector field \( Q\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  = {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } \) lies in the interior of the tangent cone of \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( s\right) \) at \( \mathbf{R} \) for all \( s \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Then for any \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and \( {h}_{0} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) there exists a closed convex \( \mathrm{O}\left( n\right) \) -invariant subset \( F \subset \; {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) with the following properties:

(1) \( F \) is preserved by the ODE \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{R} = {\mathbf{R}}^{2} + {\mathbf{R}}^{\# } \) ;

(2) \( {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( \varepsilon \right)  \cap  \left\{  {\mathbf{R} : \operatorname{trace}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\}   \subset  F \subset  {C}_{ \bullet  }\left( \varepsilon \right) \) ;

(3) \( \overline{F \smallsetminus  {C}_{\clubsuit }\left( s\right) } \) is compact (i.e., bounded) for all \( s \in  \lbrack \varepsilon ,1) \) .
